The column selection spring_wheat:peas means every column from spring_wheat through peas. The result has one row per RM-year-crop and six times as many rows as the wide table.
pivot_wider() goes in the other direction. names_from supplies the new column names and values_from supplies the values placed under them:


# Return the crop column to six separate crop columns
yields_long |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = crop,
    values_from = yield_bu_ac
  )

> # Return the crop column to six separate crop columns
> yields_long |>
+   pivot_wider(
+     names_from = crop,
+     values_from = yield_bu_ac
+   )
# A tibble: 2,950 × 8
    year    rm spring_wheat durum canola barley  oats  peas
   <dbl> <dbl>        <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
 1  2015     1         34.3  29.2   28.6   51.0  56.4  37.7
 2  2016     1         40.5  38.4   32.1   68.1  75.7  26.2
 3  2017     1         46.0  NA     39.2   NA    85.8  43.4
 4  2018     1         50    NA     39.2   76    96    42  
 5  2019     1         50.9  NA     32.4   83.5 102.   43.8
 6  2020     1         56    NA     39.9   94   120.   48.4
 7  2021     1         46.2  NA     33.2   63.7  84    37.7
 8  2022     1         52.4  NA     37.4   90.3 106.   47.4
 9  2023     1         50.8  NA     36.8   53    55.1  44.9
10  2024     1         46.7  NA     36.4   77.1  99.4  40.1
# ℹ 2,940 more rows



Analysis often uses the long form, while a report may use the wide form.


9.3.2 Awkward Column Names
Column names such as Yield (bu/ac), REGION_NAME and Field ID Number are cumbersome in code. This book uses snake case: lower-case words separated by underscores, such as yield_bu_ac, region_name and field_id.
Use rename() when only a few names need changing. The new name goes on the left and the old name on the right:


# Make a small table with awkward names
awkward_names <- tibble(
  `Weight (t)` = c(42.1, 37.8),
  CROP_NAME = c("Canola", "Wheat")
)

awkward_names |>
  rename(
    weight_tonnes = `Weight (t)`,
    crop = CROP_NAME
  )

> # Make a small table with awkward names
> awkward_names <- tibble(
+   `Weight (t)` = c(42.1, 37.8),
+   CROP_NAME = c("Canola", "Wheat")
+ )
> 
> awkward_names |>
+   rename(
+     weight_tonnes = `Weight (t)`,
+     crop = CROP_NAME
+   )
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  weight_tonnes crop  
          <dbl> <chr> 
1          42.1 Canola
2          37.8 Wheat 



janitor::clean_names() converts every name in a data frame to snake case. The package is installed once with install.packages("janitor"), then loaded in each new R session with library(janitor).


# Clean every column name in one call
awkward_names |>
  clean_names() |>
  names()

deliveries <- deliveries |> clean_names()

> # Clean every column name in one call
> awkward_names |>
+   clean_names() |>
+   names()
[1] "weight_t"  "crop_name"
> 
> deliveries <- deliveries |> clean_names()





9.3.3 Text in a Numeric Column
The first glimpse() reported weight_tonnes as <chr>, or character text. One row contains "38.2 t", so read_csv() could not treat the whole column as numeric. Find the values containing something other than a number, decimal point or minus sign:


# Find weights containing a unit or other text
deliveries |>
  filter(str_detect(weight_tonnes, "[^0-9.-]")) |>
  select(ticket_id, weight_tonnes)

> # Find weights containing a unit or other text
> deliveries |>
+   filter(str_detect(weight_tonnes, "[^0-9.-]")) |>
+   select(ticket_id, weight_tonnes)
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  ticket_id weight_tonnes
  <chr>     <chr>        
1 T0039     38.2 t       



The file was constructed with every weight in tonnes, so the suffix can be removed. In real work, that fact must come from a data dictionary or the person who made the file. parse_number() keeps the numeric part:


# Convert the weight column after checking its units
deliveries <- deliveries |>
  mutate(weight_tonnes = parse_number(weight_tonnes))

glimpse(deliveries)

> # Convert the weight column after checking its units
> deliveries <- deliveries |>
+   mutate(weight_tonnes = parse_number(weight_tonnes))
> 
> glimpse(deliveries)
Rows: 62
Columns: 6
$ ticket_id     <chr> "T0001", "T0002", "T0003", "T0004", "T0005", "T0006", "T…
$ delivery_date <chr> "2025-09-07", "2025-11-25", "2025-09-23", "15/10/2025", …
$ crop          <chr> "barley", "Peas", "barley", "canola", "Peas", "Spring wh…
$ weight_tonnes <dbl> 44.0, 44.8, 38.0, 34.7, 42.2, -12.4, 29.5, 48.1, 39.2, 4…
$ moisture_pct  <dbl> 10.400, 7.500, 10.200, 7.000, 9.000, 9.700, 9.300, NA, 8…
$ grade         <dbl> 3, 3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 2,…



If the suffix indicated a different unit, removing it would give the wrong answer. Convert the value to the common unit before discarding the label.


9.3.4 Duplicates
An exact duplicate repeats the entire row. duplicated() finds the later copy, while distinct() keeps one copy of every unique row:


# Show exact duplicates
deliveries |>
  get_dupes()

nrow(deliveries)

# Keep one copy of each unique row
deliveries <- deliveries |> distinct()
nrow(deliveries)

> # Show exact duplicates
> deliveries |>
+   get_dupes()
No variable names specified - using all columns.
# A tibble: 2 × 7
  ticket_id delivery_date crop  weight_tonnes moisture_pct grade dupe_count
  <chr>     <chr>         <chr>         <dbl>        <dbl> <dbl>      <int>
1 T0012     2025-09-24    Peas           28.9          7.8     2          2
2 T0012     2025-09-24    Peas           28.9          7.8     2          2
> 
> nrow(deliveries)
[1] 62
> 
> # Keep one copy of each unique row
> deliveries <- deliveries |> distinct()
> nrow(deliveries)
[1] 61



A conflicting duplicate repeats an identifier but not the whole row. Ticket T0030 appears with two different weights, so distinct() keeps both. Count the identifier to find it:


# Find and inspect repeated ticket numbers
deliveries |>
  get_dupes(ticket_id)

> # Find and inspect repeated ticket numbers
> deliveries |>
+   get_dupes(ticket_id)
# A tibble: 2 × 7
  ticket_id dupe_count delivery_date crop   weight_tonnes moisture_pct grade
  <chr>          <int> <chr>         <chr>          <dbl>        <dbl> <dbl>
1 T0030              2 2025-10-23    Barley          38.8          9.6     1
2 T0030              2 2025-10-23    Barley          43            9.6     1



The data alone does not say which row is correct. Check the source record. If that is impossible, report how the conflict was handled.


9.3.5 Impossible Values
Every numeric variable has a possible range. A delivery weight cannot be negative and a moisture percentage cannot be 250. summary() is a quick way to inspect the minimum and maximum:


# Inspect the ranges of the numeric measurements
deliveries |>
  select(weight_tonnes, moisture_pct) |>
  summary()

# Display values outside their possible ranges
deliveries |>
  filter(weight_tonnes <= 0 | moisture_pct > 100) |>
  select(ticket_id, weight_tonnes, moisture_pct)

> # Inspect the ranges of the numeric measurements
> deliveries |>
+   select(weight_tonnes, moisture_pct) |>
+   summary()
 weight_tonnes     moisture_pct    
 Min.   :-12.40   Min.   :  0.086  
 1st Qu.: 32.90   1st Qu.:  8.150  
 Median : 38.80   Median :  9.500  
 Mean   : 36.58   Mean   : 13.220  
 3rd Qu.: 42.90   3rd Qu.: 10.500  
 Max.   : 49.80   Max.   :250.000  
                  NAs    :2        
> 
> # Display values outside their possible ranges
> deliveries |>
+   filter(weight_tonnes <= 0 | moisture_pct > 100) |>
+   select(ticket_id, weight_tonnes, moisture_pct)
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  ticket_id weight_tonnes moisture_pct
  <chr>             <dbl>        <dbl>
1 T0006             -12.4          9.7
2 T0018              41.6        250  
3 T0043               0           10.2



A negative weight may be a sign error or a reversed transaction. A moisture value of 250 may have lost its decimal point. Those are possible explanations, not facts. Correct a value only when the source supports the correction.
Here the synthetic file provides no defensible replacement values. Record that decision by treating the three impossible measurements as missing rather than silently carrying them into later summaries:


# Mark values outside the possible range as missing.
# This records a decision; it does not invent a correction.
deliveries <- deliveries |>
  mutate(
    weight_tonnes = if_else(
      weight_tonnes <= 0,
      NA,
      weight_tonnes
    ),
    moisture_pct = if_else(
      moisture_pct > 100,
      NA,
      moisture_pct
    )
  )

> # Mark values outside the possible range as missing.
> # This records a decision; it does not invent a correction.
> deliveries <- deliveries |>
+   mutate(
+     weight_tonnes = if_else(
+       weight_tonnes <= 0,
+       NA,
+       weight_tonnes
+     ),
+     moisture_pct = if_else(
+       moisture_pct > 100,
+       NA,
+       moisture_pct
+     )
+   )



An extreme value can still be valid. A canola yield of 95 bu/ac is unusual, but it may belong to a very good field. Check it against the source and, if uncertainty remains, compare the analysis with and without it.


9.3.6 Inconsistent Categories
Several spellings of the same category produce separate groups. Count each categorical column before using it in group_by():


# Count the crop names as they arrived
deliveries |>
  count(crop, sort = TRUE)

> # Count the crop names as they arrived
> deliveries |>
+   count(crop, sort = TRUE)
# A tibble: 11 × 2
   crop               n
   <chr>          <int>
 1 "Peas"            12
 2 "barley"           9
 3 "Spring wheat"     8
 4 "peas"             7
 5 "Barley"           6
 6 "spring wheat"     5
 7 "canola"           4
 8 "Canola"           3
 9 "Canola "          3
10 "CANOLA"           2
11 "Spring Wheat"     2



Capitalization and spaces can be standardized with string functions:


# Remove extra spaces and use consistent capitalization
deliveries <- deliveries |>
  mutate(crop = str_squish(crop),
         crop = str_to_title(crop))

deliveries |>
  count(crop, sort = TRUE)

> # Remove extra spaces and use consistent capitalization
> deliveries <- deliveries |>
+   mutate(crop = str_squish(crop),
+          crop = str_to_title(crop))
> 
> deliveries |>
+   count(crop, sort = TRUE)
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  crop             n
  <chr>        <int>
1 Peas            19
2 Barley          15
3 Spring Wheat    15
4 Canola          12



Synonyms require an explicit decision. This file contains none after spacing and capitalization are standardized. When documentation says that two labels mean the same thing, put that mapping in the script; for example:


# Reconcile known synonyms while leaving other values unchanged
deliveries <- deliveries |>
  mutate(crop = case_when(
    crop == "Canola/Rapeseed" ~ "Canola",
    crop == "Soybean" ~ "Soybeans",
    TRUE ~ crop
  ))

deliveries |>
  count(crop, sort = TRUE)

> # Reconcile known synonyms while leaving other values unchanged
> deliveries <- deliveries |>
+   mutate(crop = case_when(
+     crop == "Canola/Rapeseed" ~ "Canola",
+     crop == "Soybean" ~ "Soybeans",
+     TRUE ~ crop
+   ))
> 
> deliveries |>
+   count(crop, sort = TRUE)
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  crop             n
  <chr>        <int>
1 Peas            19
2 Barley          15
3 Spring Wheat    15
4 Canola          12



The output is unchanged because those two labels are illustrative and do not occur in this file. A mapping should change data only when the documented source labels are present.


9.3.7 Mixed Units
Most moisture readings in the file are percentages near 8 to 15. Three values are below 1, which is not a plausible moisture percentage here; the intended construction of this teaching file confirms that they are proportions such as 0.099 rather than 9.9. The values are numeric, so they produce no parsing error.


# Find moisture readings recorded as decimal proportions
sum(deliveries$moisture_pct < 1, na.rm = TRUE)

deliveries |>
  filter(moisture_pct < 1) |>
  select(ticket_id, moisture_pct)

# Convert decimal proportions to percentages
deliveries <- deliveries |>
  mutate(
    moisture_pct = if_else(
      moisture_pct < 1,
      moisture_pct * 100,
      moisture_pct
    )
  )

> # Find moisture readings recorded as decimal proportions
> sum(deliveries$moisture_pct < 1, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 3
> 
> deliveries |>
+   filter(moisture_pct < 1) |>
+   select(ticket_id, moisture_pct)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  ticket_id moisture_pct
  <chr>            <dbl>
1 T0010            0.099
2 T0027            0.086
3 T0050            0.09 
> 
> # Convert decimal proportions to percentages
> deliveries <- deliveries |>
+   mutate(
+     moisture_pct = if_else(
+       moisture_pct < 1,
+       moisture_pct * 100,
+       moisture_pct
+     )
+   )



This rule depends on subject knowledge: a grain moisture value below 1 percent is not plausible here. If the file contains a unit column, use that column in case_when() instead of inferring the unit from the size of the value.


9.3.8 Missing Values
R represents a missing value as NA. Most calculations involving NA return NA. The canola trial data has three fields with no rainfall reading:


# Read a file containing three missing rainfall values
trial_data <- read_csv(
  "practice/data/canola_trial.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

mean(trial_data$rainfall_mm)
mean(trial_data$rainfall_mm, na.rm = TRUE)

> # Read a file containing three missing rainfall values
> trial_data <- read_csv(
+   "practice/data/canola_trial.csv",
+   show_col_types = FALSE
+ )
> 
> mean(trial_data$rainfall_mm)
[1] NA
> mean(trial_data$rainfall_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 229.1017



The first call returns NA because three rainfall values are unknown. The second calculates the mean from the observed values. The argument na.rm = TRUE makes that decision visible. Many Excel functions skip blank cells automatically, so the missing values need to be counted separately there.

Missing values in disguise
A blank cell, "NA", "N/A", "-", "." and -999 may all mean that no value was recorded. The na argument in the first read_csv() call told R which text codes to treat as missing.
Count missing values in every column before deciding what to do with them:


# Count missing values in each column
deliveries |>
  summarise(
    across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))
  )

> # Count missing values in each column
> deliveries |>
+   summarise(
+     across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))
+   )
# A tibble: 1 × 6
  ticket_id delivery_date  crop weight_tonnes moisture_pct grade
      <int>         <int> <int>         <int>        <int> <int>
1         0             0     0             2            3     1



A numeric code such as -999 is more dangerous. R reads it as a number and includes it in calculations. summary() exposes it as an implausible minimum unless it is converted to NA when the file is read.


Working with missing values
is.na() identifies missing values and drop_na() removes rows that contain them:


# Count missing weights
sum(is.na(deliveries$weight_tonnes))

# Count rows retained after dropping any missing value
deliveries |>
  drop_na() |>
  nrow()

# Count rows retained when only analysis variables matter
deliveries |>
  drop_na(weight_tonnes, moisture_pct) |>
  nrow()

# Calculate a mean from the observed moisture readings
mean(deliveries$moisture_pct, na.rm = TRUE)

> # Count missing weights
> sum(is.na(deliveries$weight_tonnes))
[1] 2
> 
> # Count rows retained after dropping any missing value
> deliveries |>
+   drop_na() |>
+   nrow()
[1] 55
> 
> # Count rows retained when only analysis variables matter
> deliveries |>
+   drop_na(weight_tonnes, moisture_pct) |>
+   nrow()
[1] 56
> 
> # Calculate a mean from the observed moisture readings
> mean(deliveries$moisture_pct, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 9.606897



The impossible-value decision above created missing values: there are now two missing weights and three missing moisture readings. The mean excludes the flagged moisture value of 250 rather than allowing it to distort the result. Dropping every incomplete row can remove far more data than dropping rows missing the variables used in a particular calculation.


When is dropping safe?
The answer depends on whether the chance a value is missing depends on the value itself. If a rain gauge failed at arbitrary times, the observed days may still represent the season, although there are fewer of them. If low-yielding farms were less likely to report, the remaining records will overstate average yield. In the deliveries file, omitting the three missing moisture readings would be less concerning if records were left blank for administrative reasons than if unusually wet loads were more likely to go unrecorded. Record how many values were missing, which observations were excluded and why the exclusion seemed reasonable.



9.3.9 Dates Stored as Text
glimpse() reported delivery_date as <chr> because most rows use 2025-09-07 while two use day/month/year. Text dates sort alphabetically and cannot be used in date arithmetic.
Parse the expected format and inspect the rows that fail. lubridate::ymd() warns when a value does not follow year-month-day order:


# Parse dates written as year-month-day
deliveries_with_dates <- deliveries |>
  mutate(date_parsed = lubridate::ymd(delivery_date))

# Display dates written in a different format
deliveries_with_dates |>
  filter(is.na(date_parsed)) |>
  select(ticket_id, delivery_date)

> # Parse dates written as year-month-day
> deliveries_with_dates <- deliveries |>
+   mutate(date_parsed = lubridate::ymd(delivery_date))
Warning: There was 1 warning in `mutate()`.
ℹ In argument: `date_parsed = lubridate::ymd(delivery_date)`.
Caused by warning:
!  2 failed to parse.
> 
> # Display dates written in a different format
> deliveries_with_dates |>
+   filter(is.na(date_parsed)) |>
+   select(ticket_id, delivery_date)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  ticket_id delivery_date
  <chr>     <chr>        
1 T0004     15/10/2025   
2 T0047     03/11/2025   



The value 03/11/2025 is ambiguous on its own. The other exceptional value, 15/10/2025, can only be day/month/year, and all deliveries occur from September through November, so the teaching file’s intended convention is day/month/year for both exceptional rows. Parse each stated format and combine the results:


deliveries <- deliveries |>
  mutate(
    delivery_date = coalesce(
      lubridate::ymd(delivery_date, quiet = TRUE),
      lubridate::dmy(delivery_date, quiet = TRUE)
    )
  )

deliveries |>
  select(ticket_id, delivery_date) |>
  filter(ticket_id %in% c("T0004", "T0047"))

glimpse(deliveries$delivery_date)

> deliveries <- deliveries |>
+   mutate(
+     delivery_date = coalesce(
+       lubridate::ymd(delivery_date, quiet = TRUE),
+       lubridate::dmy(delivery_date, quiet = TRUE)
+     )
+   )
> 
> deliveries |>
+   select(ticket_id, delivery_date) |>
+   filter(ticket_id %in% c("T0004", "T0047"))
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  ticket_id delivery_date
  <chr>     <date>       
1 T0004     2025-10-15   
2 T0047     2025-11-03   
> 
> glimpse(deliveries$delivery_date)
 Date[1:61], format: "2025-09-07" "2025-11-25" "2025-09-23" "2025-10-15" "2025-10-16" ...



The choice of day/month/year comes from the file’s construction and context, not from the ambiguous value alone. The final check is that the column is <date>, not <chr> (Section 7.5.2).
Once the checks are complete, write a derived file rather than editing the raw input:
write_csv(
  deliveries,
  "data/processed/grain_deliveries_clean.csv"
)
The raw file remains unchanged, the script records every decision, and rerunning it regenerates the clean file—the same principle as Refresh in Power Query.

title: 9  Cleaning Data
text:
9.4 A Checklist
Use these checks on a new file:

Use glimpse() to check the dimensions, column names and types.
Write down what one row represents and whether the table is tidy.
Use summary() to inspect the ranges of numeric variables.
Use count() on categorical variables and look for spelling and spacing differences.
Check for exact duplicates and repeated identifiers.
Count NAs in every column and look for other missing-value codes.
Check that units are consistent and dates were read as dates.
Record every correction, exclusion and assumption in the script or Power Query steps.





Wickham, Hadley, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund. 2023. R for Data Science. Second. O’Reilly Media. https://r4ds.hadley.nz/.

title: 10  Graphing Best Practices
text:
Learning Objectives
A chart asks the reader to compare positions, lengths, areas or colours instead of reading a table of numbers. It is useful when that comparison reveals a pattern more quickly than the table would.
Figure 10.1 records Napoleon’s 1812 invasion of Russia. The width of the band represents the size of the army, its position follows the route, and the line below records temperature during the retreat. The tan band begins with 422,000 men crossing into Russia. The black band returns with 10,000. Tufte called it one of the best statistical graphics ever drawn (Tufte 2001).
Figure 10.2 was published by the Georgia Department of Public Health in May 2020. It appears to show COVID-19 cases falling steadily in the five counties with the most confirmed cases.
The dates along the horizontal axis are out of order. They were sorted by case count, so the decline is built into the chart rather than present in the data. The labels contain the information needed to catch the problem, but only a reader who checks every date will find it.
These examples set the two jobs of a chart. It should make the comparison easy to see, and it should represent the data honestly.

title: 10  Graphing Best Practices
text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

State the comparison a chart is meant to show.
Choose a chart type that fits that comparison.
Label a chart so that it can be read without its maker present.
Remove clutter and use colour, text and legends deliberately.
Identify axis choices and chart forms that can mislead a reader.

title: 10  Graphing Best Practices
text:
10.1 General Principles

Decide whether a chart helps
Two numbers can usually be written in a sentence: In 2024 the United States produced 53.7 million tonnes of wheat and Canada produced 34.9 million. Turning them into two bars makes the reader estimate values that the sentence could have given directly.








Figure 10.3: Two values that are easier to state in a sentence.





The top fifteen producers make a different comparison. The chart shows Canada’s position, the gap between the first three countries and the rest, and the closeness of Canada and Australia.








Figure 10.4: The top fifteen wheat-producing countries, 2024/25. Canada is highlighted. Approximate figures from USDA.





A chart helps when the question concerns a ranking, a trend, a distribution or a relationship. If the point is one or two exact values, use prose or a small table.


Check the scale and order
Charts can mislead without containing a false number. The Georgia chart did it by changing the order of the dates. A truncated axis can do it by changing what the length of a bar represents.
Both panels below show the same five malting barley varieties, with yields from 103 to 114 bushels per acre.











(a) A. Axis starting at 100











(b) B. Axis starting at zero







Figure 10.5: The same five yields with the axis beginning at 100 and at zero.



In panel A the bars encode yield minus 100. A yield of 103 becomes a bar of length 3 and a yield of 114 becomes a bar of length 14, making a 10% yield difference look more than four times as large. Bar charts should normally begin at zero because their values are read from bar length.
Excel chooses axis bounds automatically and may produce panel A by default when the values are close together. For a column chart, right-click the value axis, choose Format Axis, and set the Minimum bound to 0. The zero baseline displays the size difference honestly, but it does not establish that small differences between trial averages are meaningful.
Line charts are different. A line shows position rather than length, so its vertical axis does not always need to begin at zero. The displayed range should still be wide enough that ordinary movement does not look like a crisis.


Use descriptive labels
A title should say what the chart shows. Axis labels should name the variables and their units. A caption should identify the source and any definition the reader needs. Yield is incomplete when the value could mean bushels per acre, kilograms per hectare or pounds per acre.
When a figure appears in a report, use the document’s caption rather than repeating the same title inside the chart. A chart copied out of the report may need its own title and source.


Remove clutter
Gridlines, borders, markers and decoration all compete with the data. Keep the elements that help the comparison and remove the rest.











(a) A. Cluttered











(b) B. Reduced







Figure 10.6: The same four series before and after unnecessary chart elements are removed.



Three-dimensional effects distort length and area. Patterned fills were useful when charts had to be printed in black and white, but on a screen they make the bars harder to read.











(a) A. Patterned fills











(b) B. Flat fills







Figure 10.7: Patterned and flat fills applied to the same bars.





Label lines directly
A legend makes the reader match each line to a separate key. When there is room, put the series name at the end of the line instead.






A. Labels placed beside the lines.







B. The same lines identified with a legend.





Legends are still useful when there are many marks, when direct labels would overlap, or when the same symbols appear in several panels.


Annotate what needs explanation
A short note can explain an unusual point or change. Too many notes hide the series they are meant to explain.











(a) A. Every movement annotated











(b) B. The unusual movement annotated







Figure 10.8: Indicative nitrogen fertilizer prices, USD per tonne, with many annotations and with one.



The second panel leaves ordinary changes alone and identifies the movement most readers would stop at.


Add variables carefully
Position on the horizontal and vertical axes carries two variables. Colour, shape and point size can carry more. In Figure 10.9, point size represents spring wheat seeded acres in addition to wheat and barley yield.








Figure 10.9: Wheat yield, barley yield and spring wheat seeded acres for Saskatchewan risk zones.





Point size is good for broad comparisons such as large, medium and small. It is poor for reading exact values because people do not judge area very precisely.
Avoid putting two different vertical scales on the same panel. Both charts below contain the same canola yield and acreage data. Only the right-hand scale changes.











(a) A. First right-hand scale











(b) B. Second right-hand scale







Figure 10.10: The same two series under two choices for the right-hand axis.



The apparent crossing point and distance between the lines are controlled by the two scales. Use separate panels or convert both series to an index when their units differ.
In Excel, this is the Combo Chart with the Secondary Axis box selected, and Recommended Charts may suggest it when the series have different magnitudes. Prefer two aligned charts or calculate each series as an index relative to its first year so both can share one scale.


Use colour for a reason
Colour can distinguish groups, show an ordered scale or draw attention to one observation. Most categories can remain grey while the category under discussion is highlighted. If every bar has a different bright colour, none has emphasis.
Choose colours that remain distinguishable for readers with colour-vision deficiencies and when printed in grey. Do not use red and green as the only signal; add labels, position or shape.

title: 10  Graphing Best Practices
text:
10.2 Types of Charts
Choose a chart from the comparison the reader needs to make. The examples below use sask_variety_yields.csv, a synthetic AREC 261 teaching dataset with risk-zone, crop, variety, year, seeded-acre and yield observations for 2021–2025. The charts aggregate the variety rows into acreage-weighted averages. A risk zone is an SCIC crop-insurance region, but these teaching values should not be presented as published SCIC estimates.

Bar charts: compare categories
A bar chart compares a value across categories such as yield by crop, acres by region or revenue by customer.








Figure 10.11: Average yield by crop, 2021–2025, bu/ac.





Sort bars by value unless the categories have a natural order. Start the value axis at zero. Horizontal bars give long category names enough room.
Excel calls vertical bars a Column chart and horizontal bars a Bar chart. Switch between them with Chart Design > Change Chart Type. Excel places the first category at the bottom of a horizontal bar chart; after sorting largest-first, use Format Axis > Axis Options > Categories in reverse order if the largest bar should appear at the top.











(a) A. Vertical











(b) B. Horizontal







Figure 10.12: The same five varieties drawn with vertical and horizontal bars.



Vertical bars work when labels are short. Use a horizontal bar chart when labels would otherwise be rotated or crowded.


Line charts: show change over time
A line chart shows movement over a continuous scale, usually time. The connection between points implies that the order and interval have meaning.
Excel Line charts normally space categories evenly, even when years are missing. For uneven intervals, use an XY Scatter chart with lines or set a recognized date axis under Format Axis > Axis Type.








Figure 10.13: Average crop yield by year, with labels at the right-hand ends of the lines.





Do not connect unordered categories such as Barley, Canola and Oats with a line.


Scatter plots: compare two numeric variables
A scatter plot places one numeric variable on each axis and one observation at each point.








Figure 10.14: Spring wheat and barley yield in Saskatchewan’s 21 risk zones.





The points rise from left to right in this 2025 cross-section. Both crops in a zone shared the same growing season, so the pattern says little by itself about whether zones that are good for wheat are generally good for barley. Module 7 develops the numerical tools for describing relationships like this.


Stacked and grouped bars: compare composition
A stacked bar shows a total and its components.








Figure 10.15: Seeded acres by crop and year, drawn as stacked bars.





Only the bottom segment has a common baseline. The middle and top segments are harder to compare across years. Grouped bars give each component a zero baseline, but they become crowded as the number of groups grows.








Figure 10.16: The same acreage data drawn as grouped bars.





When the grouped chart becomes busy, divide it into small multiples, with one panel per series.








Figure 10.17: The acreage data divided into one panel per crop.





Shared axes support comparisons of levels across panels. Free axes make the shape within each panel easier to see but prevent direct comparisons of height.
Excel does not create small multiples automatically. Make one chart, copy it for the other crops, change each copy’s series, and set identical Minimum and Maximum axis bounds. This is a case where R’s facet_wrap() requires less manual work.


Pie charts: show a simple share
A pie chart shows parts of a total. Angles and areas are harder to compare than lengths, so a bar chart is usually better when the differences matter.











(a) A. Pie











(b) B. Bars







Figure 10.18: The same four acreage shares shown as a pie and as bars.



The pie shows that canola accounts for about half of the acres seeded to these four crops. The bars make the smaller differences easier to compare. If a pie is used, keep the number of slices small, label them directly and leave it two-dimensional.


Histograms and box plots: show distributions
A histogram shows the shape of one numeric variable by counting observations in intervals. A box plot shows the median, the middle half and potential outliers in a compact form. Use a histogram when the shape matters and a box plot when several groups need to be compared (Section 3.4).


Ranges, trend lines and reference lines
A line of averages can be shown with a shaded range behind it. The range might represent a minimum and maximum, a middle percentage of observations or an interval estimate. Its definition belongs in the caption.











(a) A. Shaded range











(b) B. Fitted line







Figure 10.19: Average spring wheat yield with the middle 80% of risk zones shaded, and a scatter plot with a fitted line.



A fitted line summarizes the pattern in a scatter plot. The grey band in panel B is a 95% confidence interval for the fitted mean; later modules develop what that means. Use a fitted line when the relationship is the question and do not extend it beyond the observed data without a reason.
A reference line can show an average, a target, a break-even value or last year’s result. A waterfall chart shows how additions and subtractions turn a starting value into an ending value.
Excel provides Trendline, Histogram, Box and Whisker, and Waterfall directly. In a Waterfall chart, right-click the starting and ending bars and choose Set as Total. A reference line usually requires a helper column containing the constant value; a shaded range requires additional area-series columns.











(a) A. Reference line











(b) B. Waterfall







Figure 10.20: Canola yield against its five-year average, and a waterfall from revenue to net margin.



Dot plots can replace bars in long category lists. Heatmaps use colour to show patterns in a grid. Maps are suited to values reported by region and return in AREC 262.


Choosing



Comparison
Chart




Values across categories
Bar chart


Change over time
Line chart


Relationship between two numeric variables
Scatter plot


Components of a total
Stacked bar or bars for the components


Movement of several series
Small multiples


Distribution of one variable
Histogram or box plot


Contributions from a starting value to an ending value
Waterfall



If the chart type is hard to choose, state the comparison more precisely before opening the chart menu.

title: 10  Graphing Best Practices
text:
10.3 Excel and R for Charts
Excel is convenient for a one-off chart that will be edited in a workbook or passed to someone who does not use R. A chart updates when cells in its source range change; using an Excel Table also extends the source when new rows are added. Right-click Save as Template to reuse formatting across charts.
R is useful when the chart must be recreated from a script, updated with new data, repeated for many groups or given the same formatting as a set of other figures. The next two chapters make comparable charts in Excel and with ggplot2.




Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. 2020. COVID-19 Data Misrepresented by Georgia Health Department. Columbia Law School. https://climate.law.columbia.edu/content/covid-19-data-misrepresented-georgia-health-department.


Tufte, Edward R. 2001. The Visual Display of Quantitative Information. Second. Graphics Press.

title: 11  Graphing in Excel
text:
Learning Objectives
Excel creates a chart from a range of cells. The important part happens before the chart menu opens: decide what one row represents, calculate the values the chart needs, and arrange them in the order the reader should see.
The examples use sixty hypothetical canola fields. They build a bar chart of mean yield by region, a line chart of mean yield by year and a scatter plot of field size against yield.

title: 11  Graphing in Excel
text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Arrange a worksheet table for a bar, line or scatter chart.
Create a chart from a selected range.
Add a descriptive title and state the units.
Change an axis without making the comparison misleading.
Decide when a legend, data labels or direct labels are needed.
Copy a chart into a document or save it as an image.

title: 11  Graphing in Excel
text:
11.1 Start With the Table
A chart reads the cells you select. If those cells contain raw field records when the question concerns regional averages, summarize first. A chart cannot decide which calculation the question requires.
The bar chart has three bars, so its source table has three rows: one region and one mean per row. The line chart has one row per year. The scatter plot uses the raw observations because each field is meant to appear as one point.



Region
Mean yield (bu/ac)
Fields with yield




Central
47.6
19


North
47.3
19


South
42.7
19



Three of the sixty fields have no recorded yield. AVERAGEIF omits those blanks, and a scatter plot draws no point for them, so these charts represent 57 fields. Each regional mean summarizes fields whose yields vary substantially; the 0.3 bu/ac difference between Central and North should not be treated as a meaningful ranking without examining that variation.
Use =AVERAGEIF(Data[region],A2,Data[yield_bu_acre]) when the raw data is an Excel Table named Data. A structured reference expands as rows are added. If a summary cell shows #DIV/0! or the chart is blank, check whether the supposed numeric source column was imported as text (Section 9.3.3).

title: 11  Graphing in Excel
text:
11.2 Create a Chart
Select the table, including its headers, and use the Insert tab to choose a chart type. Excel normally uses a text first column as categories, but it may treat a numeric first column—such as Year—as another series. Use Chart Design > Select Data, remove Year from the series list, and set the Year cells as the Horizontal (Category) Axis Labels.
For the three charts in the workbook:

The bar chart selects region and mean yield, then uses a column chart for vertical bars or a bar chart for horizontal bars.
The line chart selects year and mean yield, then uses a line chart with markers.
The scatter plot selects acres and yield, then uses an XY scatter chart. A line chart is not a substitute here because field size is a measured number rather than an ordered label.

The chart remains linked to its cells. Editing the source values changes the chart; pasting new values outside a plain selected range may not. An Excel Table expands when rows are added and is usually a better source for a chart that will receive new data.
The two-year line chart is useful for learning the mechanics, but two values are more honestly reported as a sentence: mean yield was 45.8 bu/ac in 2024 and 46.0 bu/ac in 2025. A substantive trend chart needs more years.

title: 11  Graphing in Excel
text:
11.3 Titles, Axes and Legends
Use Chart Design > Add Chart Element to add or remove titles, axis labels, legends and data labels. A useful chart title describes the comparison and includes the unit when the axes do not make it obvious: Average field yield by region (bu/ac).
Bar charts normally need a zero baseline. Select the value axis, right-click Format Axis, and under Axis Options > Bounds set Minimum to 0. Mac users use the Chart Design tab for chart elements; the + button beside a selected chart is Windows-only. A line chart may use a narrower vertical range because its values are positions connected through time rather than lengths measured from a baseline (General Principles, Section 10.1), but the chosen bounds should be reported and checked.
Excel draws bars in the order of the source rows. Sort the summary table to change their order; for a horizontal bar chart, use Format Axis > Categories in reverse order to place the first row at the top.
A legend is needed when colour or shape identifies several series. A one-series chart does not need a legend that says Mean yield; the title and axis already say that. For a few lines, direct labels can be clearer than a legend.
Data labels are useful when the exact values matter and there are only a few marks. Labelling every point in a scatter plot usually hides the pattern.

title: 11  Graphing in Excel
text:
11.4 Formatting the Chart
Excel’s default chart is a starting point. Remove borders, gridlines or colours that do not help the comparison. Keep light horizontal gridlines when readers need to estimate values from the axis. Avoid three-dimensional effects, shadows and patterned fills.
Colour can identify a group or highlight one result. It does not need to change for every bar. Keep the same colour meaning across charts in the same report.
To change the size or typeface of an element, click the element itself before formatting it. This avoids changing the whole chart when only the axis labels need attention.

title: 11  Graphing in Excel
section: 11.5 Moving a Chart Into a Report
text:
11.5 Moving a Chart Into a Report
Copying a chart from Excel into Word or PowerPoint gives several paste options. The Picture option—or Paste Special > Picture (PNG)—fixes its appearance and prevents later workbook edits from changing the document. A linked chart updates from the workbook but can break when the files are moved or sent to someone else.
Desktop Excel can also use Save as Picture from a chart’s right-click menu; Excel for the web cannot. PNG works for web pages and slides. Use enough width that the labels remain readable at the size used in the report.
Before handing it over, check the source range, category order, axis minimum, labels and units. Compare one plotted value with its source cell.

title: 12  Graphing in R
text:
Learning Objectives
Excel starts with a selected range and a chart menu. In R, we describe the chart in code: the data, the variables assigned to visual properties, and the marks to draw. The ggplot2 package turns that description into a figure.
The examples use field_yields.csv, with one row for each of sixty hypothetical canola fields.
The file is simulated for teaching, so its patterns are not facts about canola. Three fields have no recorded yield.

title: 12  Graphing in R
text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Build a plot with ggplot(), aes() and a geom.
Choose a geom for a comparison, trend, relationship or distribution.
Distinguish mapping an aesthetic to a variable from setting it to a constant.
Add titles, axis labels and a theme.
Divide a plot into small multiples with facets.
save a plot with ggsave().

title: 12  Graphing in R
text:
12.1 The Grammar of Graphics
ggplot2 follows the grammar of graphics. A plot is assembled from a few parts:

Data: the data frame to plot.
Aesthetic mappings: columns assigned to position, colour, size or shape.
Geometries: points, lines, bars, boxes and other marks.
Scales: the rules connecting data values to axis positions or colours.
Facets: separate panels for groups.

Some geoms also calculate a statistic. A histogram bins values before drawing bars, and a smooth fits a line or curve before drawing it.

title: 12  Graphing in R
text:
12.2 A First Plot
This scatter plot places field size on the horizontal axis and yield on the vertical axis:

ggplot(yields, aes(x = acres, y = yield_bu_acre)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 3 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).








Figure 12.1: Field size and canola yield for sixty hypothetical fields.





Read the code in three parts:

ggplot(yields, ...) names the data frame.
aes(x = acres, y = yield_bu_acre) maps two columns to position.
geom_point() draws one point for each row with both values present.

Layers are joined with +. A pipe passes a data object into a function; the + adds a layer to a ggplot object.
The warning says that three rows were removed because their yields are missing. It is information, not an error. Once you have verified that the count is expected, na.rm = TRUE suppresses the message. Excel drops blank values from a chart without reporting how many it omitted.

title: 12  Graphing in R
text:
12.3 Common Geoms

geom_point(): scatter plots
Use points for the relationship between two numeric variables. The alpha argument makes overlapping points partly transparent.

ggplot(yields, aes(x = acres, y = yield_bu_acre)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, na.rm = TRUE)







Figure 12.2: Transparency makes overlapping observations easier to see.







geom_line(): change over time
A line chart needs one value for each point along the horizontal axis. The field file has only two years, which is not enough to show a meaningful trend, so use the ten-year RM-yield series from Module 3:

annual_mean <- read_csv(
  "practice/data/rm_yields_2015_2024.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Canola, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  rename(year = Year)

ggplot(annual_mean, aes(x = year, y = mean_yield)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2024)







Figure 12.3: Mean published RM canola yield, 2015–2024.





The summary creates one row per year. geom_line() connects those rows in year order, and scale_x_continuous() states the integer-year tick marks. Excel’s Line chart usually treats years as evenly spaced category labels instead.


geom_col() and geom_bar(): bars
Use geom_col() when the bar heights have already been calculated.

region_means <- yields |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(yield_bu_acre, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(region_means, aes(x = region, y = mean_yield)) +
  geom_col()







Figure 12.4: Mean field yield by region.





A bar of means hides how many fields are behind it and how much they vary. The box plot below shows the spread and is usually more informative for comparing these regions. In Excel, sort the summary table to reorder the bars.
Use geom_bar() when the desired value is the number of rows. It counts the observations in each category:

ggplot(yields, aes(x = region)) +
  geom_bar()







Figure 12.5: Number of fields in each region.





Excel has no counting chart: use COUNTIF or a PivotTable to create the counts, then chart that summary.


geom_histogram() and geom_boxplot(): distributions
A histogram shows the shape of one numeric variable. State the number of bins or the bin width rather than accepting the default without looking at it.

ggplot(yields, aes(x = yield_bu_acre)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12, na.rm = TRUE)







Figure 12.6: Distribution of recorded field yields.





With only 57 recorded yields, the apparent shape changes noticeably with 5, 12 or 30 bins; none is a uniquely true display. In Excel use Insert > Statistical Chart > Histogram, then Format Axis to set Bin width or Number of bins.
A box plot makes distributions compact enough to compare across categories.

ggplot(yields, aes(x = region, y = yield_bu_acre)) +
  geom_boxplot(na.rm = TRUE)







Figure 12.7: Field-yield distributions by region.





Excel’s Box and Whisker chart is in the same Statistical Chart menu, but it expects each group’s values in a separate column.


geom_smooth(): fitted patterns
geom_smooth(method = "lm") adds a fitted straight line and an interval around it:

ggplot(yields, aes(x = acres, y = yield_bu_acre)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )







Figure 12.8: Field size and yield with a fitted straight line.





Here the line is nearly flat and the 95% confidence band is wide: these synthetic fields show no clear relationship between field size and yield. A fitted line is drawn whether or not a clear relationship exists, so read the points and band as well as the line. In Excel use Chart Design > Add Chart Element > Trendline > Linear; Excel can display the equation and R-squared but does not add this confidence band. Module 7 explains what the line estimates.

title: 12  Graphing in R
text:
12.4 Mapping and Setting Aesthetics
Put an aesthetic inside aes() when it should depend on a variable. Put it outside aes() when every mark should receive the same value.
# Map colour to a column in the data
ggplot(yields, aes(x = acres, y = yield_bu_acre, colour = region)) +
  geom_point(na.rm = TRUE)

# Set one colour for every point
ggplot(yields, aes(x = acres, y = yield_bu_acre)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", na.rm = TRUE)









Figure 12.9: A. Colour mapped to region











Figure 12.10: B. One colour set for all points






Putting colour = "steelblue" inside aes() would ask ggplot to map the literal category "steelblue" to a colour scale, producing an unnecessary legend.
In Excel, colouring points by a category requires one series per group: restructure the data with FILTER() or a PivotTable, then use Select Data > Add for each series. The one-line aes(colour = region) is a practical advantage of ggplot2.

title: 12  Graphing in R
text:
12.5 Labels and Themes
labs() supplies the text and theme_minimal() changes the non-data elements of the plot:

ggplot(yields, aes(x = acres, y = yield_bu_acre, colour = region)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Field size and yield, by region",
    subtitle = "Sixty hypothetical Saskatchewan fields, 2024--2025",
    x = "Field size (acres)",
    y = "Yield (bu/acre)",
    colour = "Region",
    caption = "Source: synthetic AREC 261 data"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 12.11: A labelled scatter plot with region mapped to colour.





Other built-in themes include theme_classic() and theme_bw(). A theme changes the surrounding presentation; it does not change the data or mappings.

title: 12  Graphing in R
text:
12.6 Faceting
Faceting divides one plot into panels. Each panel below uses the same histogram definition for a different region:

ggplot(yields, aes(x = yield_bu_acre)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 8, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ region) +
  labs(x = "Yield (bu/acre)", y = "Fields")







Figure 12.12: One yield histogram for each region.





facet_grid(region ~ variety) creates a two-dimensional grid. Use it only when the resulting number of panels remains readable.
Excel has no direct faceting feature. Use a PivotChart with a slicer to view one group at a time, or build one chart per group and set identical axis bounds manually.

title: 12  Graphing in R
text:
12.7 Saving Plots
Assigning a plot to a name before ggsave() makes the saved object explicit and lets you reuse it. Create the destination folder first:


# Build and save the regional box plot
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)

region_plot <- ggplot(
  yields,
  aes(x = region, y = yield_bu_acre)
) +
  geom_boxplot(na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Yield (bu/acre)")

ggsave(
  "output/region_boxplot.png",
  plot = region_plot,
  width = 6,
  height = 4,
  dpi = 300
)

> # Build and save the regional box plot
> dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
> 
> region_plot <- ggplot(
+   yields,
+   aes(x = region, y = yield_bu_acre)
+ ) +
+   geom_boxplot(na.rm = TRUE) +
+   labs(x = NULL, y = "Yield (bu/acre)")
> 
> ggsave(
+   "output/region_boxplot.png",
+   plot = region_plot,
+   width = 6,
+   height = 4,
+   dpi = 300
+ )



Width and height are in inches unless another unit is supplied. PNG works for slides and web pages; PDF preserves vector lines and text for publication. SVG output requires the svglite package. Unlike Excel’s Save as Picture, ggsave() lets you state the output dimensions and resolution in code.






TipOther resources – ggplot2






R for Data Science (2nd ed.) – Chapter 1, “Data visualization” introduces ggplot(), aesthetic mappings, geoms and facets.
ggplot2 documentation – the function reference lists the arguments and examples for each geom.
RStudio cheatsheet – Data visualization with ggplot2.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
Learning Objectives
AI tools can explain an error, suggest R code and edit a whole project. They can also produce code that runs and answers the wrong question.
The practical question is whether you can check the result. A task is safer to hand to an AI when an error will be obvious or easy to test. It is riskier when a wrong answer looks plausible.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Decide whether an AI-assisted task can be checked reliably.
Explain why fluent output can still be wrong.
Distinguish a chatbot, an in-editor assistant and a coding agent.
Recognize common AI failures in agricultural data work.
Identify data that should not be sent to an external AI service.
State the course policy on AI use.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.1 What a Language Model Produces
A large language model is trained to predict and generate text from the context it receives. That training includes natural language and a great deal of code. Later training makes the model more useful at following instructions and answering questions.
The model’s wording does not measure its certainty. A correct function name and an invented one can arrive in the same tone. People often use hesitation as a clue that another person is unsure; generated text does not provide that clue reliably.
This is why an answer should be judged from its code, sources and results rather than from how confident it sounds.

title: 13  AI Tools
section: 13.2 Three Ways to Use AI for Code
text:
13.2 Three Ways to Use AI for Code
A chatbot answers in a separate window. It knows only what you include in the prompt, so it may guess at the column names, file structure and units. Describing the problem clearly is part of using it well.
An in-editor assistant can use the open script and other selected project context. It offers completions while you type and answers questions about the code. This removes some copying, but it also makes suggestions easier to accept without reading.
Copilot in Excel is an in-editor assistant available only with an eligible Copilot licence. It works best when the data are formatted as an Excel Table and can add formula columns, summaries and charts. Prefer an added formula you can inspect over an unexplained “insight,” and verify its result with a PivotTable or a calculation of your own. Access through the university may vary by account.
A coding agent can inspect files, edit them, run code, read errors and try again. The user’s job shifts toward specifying the task and reviewing the changes. An agent can test whether code runs; it cannot decide on its own whether the result answers the intended agricultural question.
This course uses chat and inline help first. Agentic tools are easier to review after you can read the scripts they produce.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.3 Understand What You Submit
Simon Willison gives a useful standard for AI-assisted programming:

“I won’t commit any code … if I couldn’t explain exactly what it does to somebody else.” (Willison 2025)

The same standard applies here. The model may have written a line, but you need to know what data it uses, what rows it removes and what result it creates. Code you do not understand is difficult to debug and impossible to defend on a test or in a report.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.4 Common Failure Modes

Invented functions and packages
A model may suggest a plausible function such as summarise_by() or read_excel_sheet() even when it does not exist. R stops with an error, so this is usually easy to find. Search the package’s official reference before installing a package or changing the script around an unfamiliar function.
In Excel, an invented or unavailable function produces #NAME?. The same error can mean that a real Microsoft 365 function is unavailable in an older Excel version, so check the function’s Microsoft support page and its version list.


Assumed column names
If the model has not seen the data, it may write code for columns named yield, crop and year. The file may use Yield, Crop_Name and Harvest_Year. Supply glimpse() output or a short description of the columns before asking for code. For Excel, supply the exact header row, two or three made-up example rows, the sheet and range, and whether the range is an Excel Table.


Out-of-date syntax
Packages change. An old function or argument may have been replaced since the model’s training data was collected. For example, gather() still appears in older code, while current tidyr uses pivot_longer(). “Superseded” means an older function still works but is no longer recommended; “deprecated” normally warns; “defunct” errors. Package documentation is the check.


Numbers produced without a reproducible calculation
Do not ask a chatbot to calculate a reported statistic from pasted rows and then trust the number. Ask for code, run it in R and keep the calculation in the script. In Excel, every reported number should come from a visible formula rather than a typed constant; use FORMULATEXT when the calculation needs to be audited.


Assumptions from another place
Answers about agriculture may default to US crops, agencies and geography. Saskatchewan data may use rural municipalities rather than counties, SCIC definitions rather than a US crop-insurance program, and bushels per acre rather than another yield unit.
Figure 13.1 shows the same 2025 canola yield in three units. A conversion error can change the numerical scale without causing an R error.








Figure 13.1: The acreage-weighted mean 2025 canola yield in the teaching variety file, reported in three units.





The failures differ in how easy they are to notice. An invented function stops the script. A wrong unit or incomplete join may not.








Figure 13.2: Common failures arranged by whether R is likely to stop the script.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.5 A Silent Failure
The yield file is synthetic teaching data, and the five round crop prices are illustrative placeholders rather than observed 2025 market prices. The question is the average 2025 revenue per acre for spring wheat, canola, barley and oats, weighted by acres; the resulting dollars demonstrate a join and are not a Saskatchewan revenue estimate.
The following code looks reasonable. It filters the yield data, joins prices by crop, calculates revenue and then uses na.rm = TRUE in the weighted mean.


# Load the two files
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))

d <- read_csv(
  "practice/data/sask_variety_yields.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
p <- read_csv(
  "practice/data/crop_prices.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Keep recorded yields for four crops in 2025
d25 <- d |>
  filter(
    Year == 2025,
    Crop %in% c(
      "Wheat - Hard Red Spring",
      "Canola/Rapeseed",
      "Barley",
      "Oats"
    ),
    !is.na(Yield),
    !is.na(Acres),
    Acres > 0
  )

# Add the price and calculate revenue per acre
j <- d25 |>
  left_join(p, by = "Crop") |>
  mutate(Revenue = Yield * Price_per_bu)

weighted.mean(j$Revenue, j$Acres, na.rm = TRUE)

> # Load the two files
> suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
> 
> d <- read_csv(
+   "practice/data/sask_variety_yields.csv",
+   show_col_types = FALSE
+ )
> p <- read_csv(
+   "practice/data/crop_prices.csv",
+   show_col_types = FALSE
+ )
> 
> # Keep recorded yields for four crops in 2025
> d25 <- d |>
+   filter(
+     Year == 2025,
+     Crop %in% c(
+       "Wheat - Hard Red Spring",
+       "Canola/Rapeseed",
+       "Barley",
+       "Oats"
+     ),
+     !is.na(Yield),
+     !is.na(Acres),
+     Acres > 0
+   )
> 
> # Add the price and calculate revenue per acre
> j <- d25 |>
+   left_join(p, by = "Crop") |>
+   mutate(Revenue = Yield * Price_per_bu)
> 
> weighted.mean(j$Revenue, j$Acres, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 476.7889



The result, $476.79 per acre, is plausible. The crop names do not all match. The price file uses Canola and Spring wheat; the yield file uses Canola/Rapeseed and Wheat - Hard Red Spring. Barley and oats match, while canola and wheat receive NA for price.
Count the failed matches before calculating anything:


nrow(d25)
nrow(j)

d25 |>
  anti_join(p, by = "Crop") |>
  distinct(Crop)

sum(is.na(j$Price_per_bu))

sum(j$Acres[is.na(j$Price_per_bu)]) / sum(j$Acres)

j |>
  count(Crop, price_missing = is.na(Price_per_bu))

> nrow(d25)
[1] 1416
> nrow(j)
[1] 1416
> 
> d25 |>
+   anti_join(p, by = "Crop") |>
+   distinct(Crop)
# A tibble: 2 × 1
  Crop                   
  <chr>                  
1 Canola/Rapeseed        
2 Wheat - Hard Red Spring
> 
> sum(is.na(j$Price_per_bu))
[1] 1051
> 
> sum(j$Acres[is.na(j$Price_per_bu)]) / sum(j$Acres)
[1] 0.8732356
> 
> j |>
+   count(Crop, price_missing = is.na(Price_per_bu))
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  Crop                    price_missing     n
  <chr>                   <lgl>         <int>
1 Barley                  FALSE           245
2 Canola/Rapeseed         TRUE            674
3 Oats                    FALSE           120
4 Wheat - Hard Red Spring TRUE            377



The join preserves all 1,416 rows, but 1,051 rows—and about 87% of the acres—have no price. na.rm = TRUE removes them from the weighted mean, so the reported value describes barley and oats rather than all four crops. Use na.rm = TRUE only after counting the missing values and explaining their source.








Figure 13.3: Rows in the 2025 yield data according to whether the join found a crop price.





Reconcile the two known names, repeat the join and check again:


# Reconcile crop names with the price table
d25_fixed <- d25 |>
  mutate(Crop = case_match(
    Crop,
    "Canola/Rapeseed" ~ "Canola",
    "Wheat - Hard Red Spring" ~ "Spring wheat",
    .default = Crop
  ))

# Repeat the join and state the expected relationship
j_fixed <- d25_fixed |>
  left_join(
    p,
    by = "Crop",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  ) |>
  mutate(Revenue = Yield * Price_per_bu)

sum(is.na(j_fixed$Price_per_bu))
stopifnot(!anyNA(j_fixed$Price_per_bu))
weighted.mean(j_fixed$Revenue, j_fixed$Acres)

> # Reconcile crop names with the price table
> d25_fixed <- d25 |>
+   mutate(Crop = case_match(
+     Crop,
+     "Canola/Rapeseed" ~ "Canola",
+     "Wheat - Hard Red Spring" ~ "Spring wheat",
+     .default = Crop
+   ))
> 
> # Repeat the join and state the expected relationship
> j_fixed <- d25_fixed |>
+   left_join(
+     p,
+     by = "Crop",
+     relationship = "many-to-one"
+   ) |>
+   mutate(Revenue = Yield * Price_per_bu)
> 
> sum(is.na(j_fixed$Price_per_bu))
[1] 0
> stopifnot(!anyNA(j_fixed$Price_per_bu))
> weighted.mean(j_fixed$Revenue, j_fixed$Acres)
[1] 571.171



The corrected result is $571.17 per acre. In Excel, XLOOKUP would expose unmatched names as #N/A; do not let an AI hide them with IFERROR(...,0), and avoid VLOOKUP without an explicit exact-match argument. Count missing results with =SUMPRODUCT(--ISNA(price_range)) before calculating revenue.
Supplying the price table’s exact crop names in the prompt could have prevented this case. The checks that catch it regardless of the prompt are anti_join(), before-and-after row counts, a missing-value count, and the stopifnot() guard.

title: 13  AI Tools
section: 13.6 Tasks That Are Easy to Check
text:
13.6 Tasks That Are Easy to Check
AI assistance is useful when the result can be tested quickly:

Explain an R error message and identify the line it refers to.
Suggest the name of a function, followed by a check of its documentation.
Draft repetitive syntax such as a case_when() block.
Explain an unfamiliar line of code.
Produce a first draft of a plot whose labels, groups and values can be inspected.
Explain an Excel error such as #SPILL!, #VALUE! or #REF!, followed by checking the referenced cells.
Draft a SUMIFS or XLOOKUP, followed by filtering the source table and checking matching rows.

In each case, R or the user provides a separate check.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.7 Tasks Requiring More Judgment
Some tasks require information the model does not have:

Choosing the analysis without a clear question.
Deciding whether the observations represent the population of interest.
Judging whether an agricultural result is plausible in its stated units and location.
Choosing which caveat matters to a producer, client or policy maker.
Supplying references that have not been checked against the original source.

AI can help list possibilities, but the final decision has to be justified from the question, data and subject matter.

title: 13  AI Tools
section: 13.8 Data That Should Not Be Sent
text:
13.8 Data That Should Not Be Sent
Prompts and code sent to a hosted AI service leave the computer. What is stored, for how long, and whether it is used to improve a service depends on the provider, account and organization settings.
The datasets in this course are public or synthetic. A producer’s field records, financial statements, contact information, employee data and material covered by a confidentiality agreement are different. Do not paste someone else’s confidential data into a consumer AI tool. Describe the column names, types and problem without supplying the values, or use a service approved by the organization that owns the data.
An in-editor assistant may use the current file or other project context. Check what context has been selected and close or exclude files that should not be sent (Section 14.4).
Copilot in Excel sends Table content to Microsoft’s service; it is not a local calculation. An organization-managed Microsoft 365 account may operate within that organization’s data protections, while a consumer chatbot account does not inherit them. Follow the data owner’s policy and use headers plus made-up rows when approval is uncertain.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.9 Course Policy
AI tools may be used for module practice and the course project. They may not be used on tests.
Tests check whether you can read the data, choose an analysis and recognize an implausible answer without the tool doing those jobs for you. For submitted work, you must be able to explain every line of code and account for every reported number.
A 2026 working paper reports an observational comparison involving 26,811 Chinese secondary students who self-selected into using generative AI (Strömberg et al. 2026). After adoption, homework scores rose and completion times fell, while exam scores fell.






Figure 13.4: Changes in homework scores, completion time and exam scores after students began using AI, compared with students who had not. Source: Strömberg, Lei and Wu (2026).



The paper argues that students substituted the tool for practice. That is a plausible interpretation, but its subgroup comparison contrasts students who chose to change their work differently; it is not a clean experimental test of the mechanism. The result therefore does not imply that every use of AI reduces learning.
Other courses have their own rules. Check the syllabus for each course before using AI on assessed work.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.10 The Rest of This Module
The next chapter sets up GitHub Copilot as a provider for Positron Assistant and develops a checking routine. The final chapter uses graphing exercises because a visible figure makes many coding errors easier to inspect. This module practises AI assistance mainly in Positron because scripts make the generated work visible; the same checking habits apply to formulas and charts produced by Copilot in Excel.






TipOther resources – AI-assisted coding






3Blue1Brown, But what is a GPT? gives a visual explanation of language-model prediction.
Simon Willison, Not all AI-assisted programming is vibe coding develops the explanation standard used above.








Strömberg, David, Victor Lei, and Yanhui Wu. 2026. The Generative AI Learning Penalty: Evidence from Chinese Secondary Education. CEPR Discussion Paper No. DP21577. Centre for Economic Policy Research. https://cepr.org/publications/dp21577.


Willison, Simon. 2025. Not All AI-Assisted Programming Is Vibe Coding (but Vibe Coding Rocks). https://simonwillison.net/2025/Mar/19/vibe-coding/.

title: 14  GitHub Copilot
text:
Learning Objectives
GitHub Copilot works inside Positron. It can complete code while you type and provide a model for Posit Assistant chat, so the assistant can work with the script and project already open in the editor.
The useful part is the context. Inline completions use text around the cursor; chat uses the selection or files you attach. It still does not know what a dataset contains unless the data or its structure is included in that context.
GitHub Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot are separate products. GitHub Copilot supplies coding help in Positron and is the product used here. Copilot in Excel requires separate Microsoft licensing; GitHub Education does not unlock it.

title: 14  GitHub Copilot
text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Connect a GitHub Copilot account to Positron.
Use inline completions and Posit Assistant chat for different tasks.
Give the assistant enough information about a dataset to avoid guessing.
Decide whether to accept, revise or reject suggested code.
Check AI-assisted code before it becomes part of an analysis.

title: 14  GitHub Copilot
text:
14.1 Getting Access
GitHub’s plan names and student eligibility change. Check the linked GitHub student-access page for what is available this term and do not enter payment information for this course.
To apply for the student benefit:

Create a personal account at github.com if you do not have one.
Open your GitHub Education benefits and start a student application.
Add and verify your @usask.ca address if GitHub asks for an academic email.
Supply current proof of enrolment, such as a student card with an enrolment date, a class schedule, a transcript or an enrolment letter.
After verification, return to the benefits page and activate the Copilot benefit. Education approval and Copilot activation are separate steps.

Apply early. Verification can take several days, and the account may not be ready on the night an assignment is due.

title: 14  GitHub Copilot
text:
14.2 Connecting Copilot to Positron
Recent versions of Positron include AI support directly. You do not need to install the GitHub Copilot extension from the Extensions pane.

Update Positron before beginning.
Open View > Command Palette, or use Cmd+Shift+P on macOS or Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows.
Run Authentication: Configure Language Model Providers.
Select GitHub Copilot and sign in through the browser window that opens.
Return to Positron and open Posit Assistant chat. Copilot should appear as an available provider.

Copilot’s grey inline completions become available after the same sign-in. If chat or completions do not appear, restart Positron. If the account was connected in an older Positron release, sign out of GitHub from the Accounts menu and sign in again.
The command AI: Create Diagnostic Report lists the active providers and AI settings without exposing the content of your prompts. It is the quickest check when Positron appears connected but produces no suggestions.
These command names were checked in August 2026. If a later Positron release uses different wording, search the Command Palette for “language model” or “AI” and consult the configuration page linked below.

title: 14  GitHub Copilot
text:
14.3 Two Ways to Use It

Inline completions
Inline completions appear as grey text while you type. Press Tab to accept a suggestion, Esc to dismiss it or keep typing to replace it.
A comment can provide a short instruction:
# Read the yield data and count rows by crop
A plausible completion might invent both the file and column name:
yields <- read_csv("yields.csv")
count(yields, crop)
Neither name was supplied by the comment. Grey text is a suggestion, not evidence that the assistant found the correct file.
Inline completion is useful for predictable syntax, repeated arguments and the next line of a pattern already present in the script. It is a poor place to ask for an explanation because the result arrives as code rather than a discussion.


Posit Assistant chat
Chat is useful for questions: why an error occurred, what a line does, how to reorganize a plot or what checks belong after a join. Select the relevant code or file before asking so the assistant receives the right context.
Posit Assistant is the default chat interface in Positron. GitHub Copilot can supply its language model after you connect the provider. This distinction matters when following documentation: Copilot is the account and model provider; Posit Assistant is the chat interface you see in Positron.

title: 14  GitHub Copilot
section: 14.4 Show the Shape of the Data
text:
14.4 Show the Shape of the Data
Copilot cannot infer a file’s columns from its filename. If it has not seen sask_variety_yields.csv, code using an assumed column name is a guess.
Run glimpse() and inspect the categories rather than typing them from memory:


suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tidyverse)
  library(janitor)
})

d <- read_csv(
  "practice/data/sask_variety_yields.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  clean_names()

glimpse(d)
d |> distinct(crop)

# d has columns: risk_zone, crop, variety, year, acres, yield

title: 14  GitHub Copilot
text:
14.5 Accepting and Rejecting
Accept code when you can explain what it does and can name the check that would reveal an error.

Usually safe to accept after reading: syntax you recognize, plotting boilerplate and repetitive argument lists.
Read and test carefully: joins, filters, grouped summaries, missing-value handling and any code that changes the number of rows.
Stop and investigate: unfamiliar functions or packages, an unexpectedly long solution or code whose result you cannot predict.
For Excel, stop at #NAME?: the function may require a newer Microsoft 365 build. Ask for a SUMIFS or INDEX/MATCH alternative when compatibility matters.

Rejecting a suggestion costs almost nothing. Accepting code you do not understand leaves you responsible for a calculation you cannot defend or repair.

title: 14  GitHub Copilot
text:
14.6 Checking the Work
Use the same checks after every AI-assisted change:

Read every line and identify which data it uses.
Count rows before and after a filter, join or grouped operation.
Test the code on a small case whose answer is known.
Recalculate one result another way.
Inspect the final table or chart against the question that was asked.

The assistant can help write a check. It cannot replace the independent evidence supplied by that check.
For the weighted-mean example, count the rows and independently recalculate one crop from its numerator and denominator:


nrow(d)
nrow(d_2025)

d_2025 |>
  filter(crop == "Barley") |>
  summarise(
    checked_mean = sum(acres * yield) / sum(acres)
  )

> nrow(d)
[1] 13625
> nrow(d_2025)
[1] 2722
> 
> d_2025 |>
+   filter(crop == "Barley") |>
+   summarise(
+     checked_mean = sum(acres * yield) / sum(acres)
+   )
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  checked_mean
         <dbl>
1         82.9



In Excel, press F2 or use Formulas > Evaluate Formula to see which cells a formula reads, compare the result with a PivotTable, copy the formula down to test relative and absolute references, compare COUNT with COUNTA to find numbers stored as text, and require exact matching in every lookup.

title: 15  Graphing with AI
text:
Learning Objectives
Graphing is a good place to begin using AI assistance. ggplot2 is consistent, but details such as annotations, direct labels and axis breaks require arguments that are easy to forget. An assistant can draft that syntax quickly.
Charts also expose many mistakes. A label beside the wrong year, a missing panel or a clipped axis can be seen. That makes the draft easier to check than a join that drops rows and still returns a plausible number.
These exercises use R because ggplot2 code is text that an assistant can draft and you can inspect. Copilot inside Excel is a separately licensed product and is not unlocked by GitHub Copilot. A browser assistant can suggest Excel steps if you provide headers and made-up rows, but you must carry out and verify the clicks yourself.

title: 15  Graphing with AI
text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Ask an AI assistant for ggplot2 code using the actual structure of a dataset.
Check the data supplied to an AI-produced chart.
Check the marks, labels, groups and scales drawn by the chart.
Recognize when repeated prompting is no longer improving the result.

title: 15  Graphing with AI
section: 15.1 A Chart Does Not Check Its Data
text:
15.1 A Chart Does Not Check Its Data
A chart can show whether the drawing is wrong. It cannot show whether the wrong rows were supplied to it.
A clean chart of 2024 is still wrong when the question asked about 2025. Code that removes every row with missing acreage may also create a convincing figure while changing the population being described.
Check both sides of the plot:

Before plotting, inspect the number of rows, groups, missing values and numerical ranges.
After plotting, inspect the marks, labels, axes and panels.

The synthetic teaching file contains one row for a variety in a risk zone and year. Its rectangular layout includes combinations with no acreage and yield, often because that variety is absent from that zone-year. Consequently, comparisons across years also compare changing sets of varieties. The file has 13,625 rows, including 4,186 with no recorded yield. Inspect the counts before drawing the figure:


suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))

d <- read_csv(
  "practice/data/sask_variety_yields.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

glimpse(d)

d |>
  summarise(
    rows = n(),
    missing_yield = sum(is.na(Yield)),
    .by = Year
  )

   Year  rows missing_yield
  <dbl> <int>         <int>
1  2021  2725          1380
2  2022  2725          1206
3  2023  2725           929
4  2024  2725           668
5  2025  2725             3











Figure 15.1: Rows with and without a recorded yield, by year.





About half the 2021 rows have no yield, while almost all 2025 rows have one. A trend therefore reflects turnover in the varieties represented as well as changes in yield. In Excel, a PivotTable with Year in Rows and both Count of Variety and Count of Yield in Values provides the same check.

title: 15  Graphing with AI
text:
15.2 The Exercises
All five exercises use sask_variety_yields.csv. Its columns are Risk_Zone, Crop, Variety, Year, Acres and Yield.
Work in Positron with an assistant connected. For each exercise, describe the result, read the proposed code, run it and complete the checks. When the draft is wrong, tell the assistant what is wrong rather than asking it to produce the same chart again.

1. Annotate one point
Plot the unweighted mean yield by year for Crop == "Wheat - Hard Red Spring". Add a note with an arrow pointing to 2021 and identify it as a drought year; that label comes from outside weather knowledge, while the file itself shows only a low-yield year.
Checks: Does the arrow point to 2021? Is the note inside the plotting area? Which Crop value did the code filter? How many recorded yields contribute to each annual point? Is the mean weighted or unweighted, and is that what you intended?


2. Replace a legend with direct labels
Plot average yield by year for Wheat - Hard Red Spring, Canola/Rapeseed, Barley and Oats. Put each crop name beside the right end of its line and remove the legend.
Checks: Are all four labels present and beside the correct line? Has a label been clipped at the panel edge? Can the series still be distinguished when printed in grey?


3. Shade a range behind a line
Plot average Wheat - Hard Red Spring yield by year and add a geom_ribbon() band showing the range across risk-zone means. Summarize first by zone-year and then by year; draw the ribbon before the line so it sits behind it.
