Answer

quantile(sw$Yield_bu_ac, c(0.25, 0.75))
IQR(sw$Yield_bu_ac)


25th 47.3, 75th 56.1; IQR 8.8 both ways.


The middle half of province-year wheat yields falls in a nine-bushel window, from about 47 to 56 bu/ac.





Question 59
A classmate on a brand-new laptop runs:
install.packages(tidyverse)
and gets Error: object 'tidyverse' not found.
(a) In a comment: what rule from the module did they break, and what is the corrected line?
(b) In a comment: after installing correctly, what line still has to appear at the top of the script, and why?
(c) The tidyverse is a collection of packages. In comments, name the four core ones from the module and the job each does.


Answer



The quotes rule – the package name is quoted when installing. Without quotes, R looks for an object called tidyverse and finds none. Corrected: install.packages("tidyverse").


library(tidyverse) – installing puts the package on the computer, but each script or session has to load it before its functions exist.


readr reads data, dplyr manipulates it, tidyr reshapes it, ggplot2 makes graphs.





Question 60
Your download folder contains sk wheat data (new) FINAL.csv.
(a) In a comment: list every violation of the module’s file-naming rules in that name, and rename it properly.
(b) In a comment: why does the module say to save the file into data/ untouched, even before you have looked at it?
(c) In a comment: if you wanted the download date in the name, how would you write it and why?


Answer



Spaces, parentheses, and a FINAL tag standing in for version control. Something like statcan_spring_wheat_2015_2025.csv.


data/ holds raw files exactly as they arrived, so there is always an untouched original to go back to; every change happens in the script, where it leaves a record.


As YYYY-MM-DD (e.g. 2026-10-08_statcan_spring_wheat.csv) so alphabetical order is also chronological order.

title: Module 2 — Test Bank
text:
Questions 61–70 · Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields
These questions use the full eight-crop file: read rm_yields_1990_2025.csv into an object called rm_yields at the start of this block.

Question 61
(a) Filter rm_yields to Canola in 2024, saving the result as canola_2024. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) From canola_2024, select only the RM and Yield columns, saving the result. Report its column names and its number of columns.
(c) In a comment: after (a) and (b), how many rows does rm_yields itself have, and why?


Answer

canola_2024 <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Canola" & Year == 2024)
nrow(canola_2024)
canola_slim <- select(canola_2024, RM, Yield)
names(canola_slim)
ncol(canola_slim)


293 rows.


RM, Yield; 2 columns (still 293 rows).


Still 71,104 – filter() and select() return new data frames and leave the original untouched.





Question 62
(a) Filter to rows where the crop is Oats or Barley, using |, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Write the same filter using %in% and confirm the row count matches.
(c) Sort your filtered data frame from highest yield to lowest. Which crop, RM, and year hold the top spot, and at what yield?
(d) In a comment: a classmate tried filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Oats" & Crop == "Barley") and got zero rows. Why?


Answer

oats_barley <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Oats" | Crop == "Barley")
nrow(oats_barley)
oats_barley2 <- filter(rm_yields, Crop %in% c("Oats", "Barley"))
nrow(oats_barley2)
arrange(oats_barley, desc(Yield))

(a, b) 19,709 rows both ways.

A tie at 165.1 bu/ac: Oats in RM 369 (2025) and Oats in RM 438 (2020) share the maximum, so either is a correct top row.


& requires both conditions true of the same row, and no single row’s crop is both Oats and Barley. “Or” is the right connector.





Question 63
(a) Filter to the Spring Wheat observations of at least 60 bu/ac (all years), using >= and saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Filter again to keep only the 2023 rows of that result. How many rows are in this second data frame?
(c) From your 2023 data frame, select RM and Yield and sort best-first. Which RM tops the list, at what yield?
(d) In a comment: rewrite the condition “yield at least 60 and the crop is not Spring Wheat” using !.


Answer

sw_60 <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Spring Wheat" & Yield >= 60)
nrow(sw_60)
sw_60_2023 <- filter(sw_60, Year == 2023)
nrow(sw_60_2023)
sw_best <- select(sw_60_2023, RM, Yield)
arrange(sw_best, desc(Yield))


434 rows. (b) 53 rows.


RM 187, at 74.7 bu/ac.


filter(rm_yields, Yield >= 60 & !Crop == "Spring Wheat").





Question 64
(a) Make a version of the data with only Year, RM, Crop, and Yield – once by naming what you keep, once by dropping what you don’t want – saving each, and confirm the two have the same column names. Then make a third version keeping the adjacent-column range Year:Crop, and report its column names.
(b) Rename Yield to yield_per_acre in the full data, saving the result, and show the new column names.
(c) Filter your renamed data frame to Peas in 2025. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?


Answer

kept    <- select(rm_yields, Year, RM, Crop, Yield)
dropped <- select(rm_yields, -Unit)
names(kept)
names(dropped)
ranged  <- select(rm_yields, Year:Crop)
names(ranged)
renamed <- rename(rm_yields, yield_per_acre = Yield)
names(renamed)
peas_2025 <- filter(renamed, Crop == "Peas" & Year == 2025)
nrow(peas_2025)


Identical: Year, RM, Crop, Yield both ways; the range version keeps Year, RM, Crop.


Year, RM, Crop, yield_per_acre, Unit.


285 rows.





Question 65
Lentil yields are in pounds per acre; one pound per acre is about 1.12 kg per hectare.
(a) Filter to the lentil rows, saving as lentils. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Use mutate() to add a yield_kg_ha column to lentils, saving the result back to lentils.
(c) Compute the mean of the new column, and the mean of the original Yield column, and check the ratio is the conversion factor.


Answer

lentils <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Lentils")
nrow(lentils)
lentils <- mutate(lentils, yield_kg_ha = Yield * 1.12)
mean(lentils$yield_kg_ha)
mean(lentils$Yield)


6,338 rows.


Mean 1,353.4 kg/ha vs 1,208.39 lb/ac – and 1353.4 / 1208.39 ≈ 1.12.





Question 66
(a) Filter to Canola in 2024, then in one mutate() call add two columns: yield_t_ha (multiply by 0.0560) and yield_kg_ha (multiply by 56.0). Save each step.
(b) Compute the mean of each new column.
(c) Sort by yield_t_ha, best first. Which RM tops the table, and at what yield in t/ha?
(d) In a comment: without running anything, what is the mean of yield_kg_ha divided by the mean of yield_t_ha, and why?


Answer

canola_2024 <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Canola" & Year == 2024)
canola_2024 <- mutate(canola_2024,
                      yield_t_ha  = Yield * 0.0560,
                      yield_kg_ha = Yield * 56.0)
mean(canola_2024$yield_t_ha)
mean(canola_2024$yield_kg_ha)
arrange(canola_2024, desc(yield_t_ha))


1.76 t/ha and 1,764.11 kg/ha.


RM 493, at 2.57 t/ha.


1,000 – both columns are the same yields scaled by constants, and 56.0 / 0.0560 = 1000 (a tonne is 1,000 kg).





Question 67
(a) Filter to Flax in 2025, saving as flax_2025. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Sort it from highest yield to lowest, and report the RM and yield in the top row.
(c) Sort it from lowest to highest instead. What changes in the code?
(d) In a comment: after (b) and (c), is flax_2025 itself now sorted? Why or why not?


Answer

flax_2025 <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Flax" & Year == 2025)
nrow(flax_2025)
arrange(flax_2025, desc(Yield))
arrange(flax_2025, Yield)


195 rows.


RM 381 at 45.5 bu/ac.


Drop the desc().


No – neither sorted result was assigned, so both were displayed and discarded; flax_2025 is unchanged.





Question 68
A script contains, in order:
filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Peas")
peas <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Peas")
(a) In a comment: what does each line do, and what appears in the console after each?
(b) Report nrow(peas) and nrow(rm_yields).
(c) In a comment: connect this to the same distinction you met with x * 3 in the console back in Section 1.


Answer



Line 1 computes the pea rows and prints them – nothing is saved. Line 2 computes the same thing and saves it as peas, printing nothing.


nrow(peas) is 9,270; nrow(rm_yields) is still 71,104.


It is displaying versus saving again: an expression’s result appears in the console and vanishes unless assigned to an object.





Question 69
(a) Filter to Canola in RM 232 (all years), saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) From that object, select only Year and Yield, saving again.
(c) Sort it so the best year is on top. Which year was it, and what was the yield?


Answer

canola_232 <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Canola" & RM == 232)
nrow(canola_232)
canola_232 <- select(canola_232, Year, Yield)
arrange(canola_232, desc(Yield))


31 rows (some years are missing – the crop was not grown or reported in that RM every year).


2016, at 43.9 bu/ac.





Question 70
(a) Using head(), display the first six rows of rm_yields.
(b) Sort the data by Yield in descending order into a new object, select its Crop, Yield, and Unit columns into another, and display the first six rows of that (leaving rm_yields unchanged throughout).
(c) In a comment: every row in (b) is the same crop. Which one, why those rows, and what would you check before comparing their values with the other crops?
(d) Now sort by Crop first and by descending Yield within each crop, into a new object, and display its first six rows. Which crop fills them, and why that crop?


Answer

head(rm_yields)
sorted <- arrange(rm_yields, desc(Yield))
top_cols <- select(sorted, Crop, Yield, Unit)
head(top_cols)
by_crop <- arrange(rm_yields, Crop, desc(Yield))
head(by_crop)

(b, c) All lentils – their yields are recorded in pounds per acre, so they dominate the top of any sort on Yield. Before comparing across crops you would check the Unit column and convert to a common unit.

All Barley – Crop sorts alphabetically first, so the display starts with Barley’s own best yields (RM 380 in 2025 at 122 bu/ac on top).

title: Module 2 — Test Bank
text:
Questions 71–80 · Manitoba Wheat Variety
These questions use the full mb_wheat_varieties.csv – including the suppressed rows, where Reported is FALSE and the numeric columns are missing. Read it into an object called mb at the start of this block.

Question 71
(a) Filter mb to the reported rows (Reported == TRUE), saving as mb_rep. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) From mb_rep, select Municipality, Variety, and Yield_bu_ac, saving the result. Report its column names.
(c) In a comment: how many rows does mb itself still have, and what happened to the suppressed rows in mb_rep?


Answer

mb_rep <- filter(mb, Reported == TRUE)
nrow(mb_rep)
mb_slim <- select(mb_rep, Municipality, Variety, Yield_bu_ac)
names(mb_slim)


2,398 rows.


Municipality, Variety, Yield_bu_ac.


mb still has 5,358 rows – filtering returns a new data frame. The 2,960 suppressed rows are simply absent from mb_rep; they were not deleted from anything.





Question 72
(a) From mb_rep (reported rows), filter to the varieties AAC BRANDON (BW 932) or AAC STARBUCK <SECAN> using |, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Write the same filter using %in% and confirm the count matches.
(c) In a comment: a classmate wrote the condition with & instead of | and got zero rows. Why?


Answer

two_var <- filter(mb_rep, Variety == "AAC BRANDON (BW 932)" | Variety == "AAC STARBUCK <SECAN>")
nrow(two_var)
two_var2 <- filter(mb_rep, Variety %in% c("AAC BRANDON (BW 932)", "AAC STARBUCK <SECAN>"))
nrow(two_var2)

(a, b) 893 rows both ways.

& demands both conditions true of the same row, and no single row’s variety is both names at once. “Or” is the right connector.





Question 73
(a) Filter mb_rep to yields above 80 bu/ac, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Filter that result again to 2024 only. How many rows now?
(c) Sort your over-80 data frame from (a) best-first. Which municipality, variety, and year top the list, at what yield?


Answer

high <- filter(mb_rep, Yield_bu_ac > 80)
nrow(high)
high_2024 <- filter(high, Year == 2024)
nrow(high_2024)
arrange(high, desc(Yield_bu_ac))


97 rows. (b) 16 rows.


HILLSBURG-ROBLIN-SHELL RIVER, BOLLES <SEED DEPOT>, in 2022, at 97.8 bu/ac.





Question 74
(a) From mb_rep, make a version with only Year, Municipality, Variety, and Yield_bu_ac – once by naming what you keep, once by dropping what you don’t (Farms, Acres, Reported) – saving each, and confirm the two have the same column names. Then make a third version keeping the adjacent range Year:Variety and report its names.
(b) Rename Yield_bu_ac to yield, saving the result, and show the new column names.


Answer

kept    <- select(mb_rep, Year, Municipality, Variety, Yield_bu_ac)
dropped <- select(mb_rep, -Farms, -Acres, -Reported)
names(kept)
names(dropped)
ranged  <- select(mb_rep, Year:Variety)
names(ranged)
renamed <- rename(mb_rep, yield = Yield_bu_ac)
names(renamed)


Identical four names both ways; the range version keeps Year, Municipality, Variety.


The same seven columns with yield in place of Yield_bu_ac.





Question 75
(a) From mb_rep, use one mutate() to add total_bu, each observation’s acres times its yield, saving the result.
(b) Compute the mean of total_bu.
(c) Sort by total_bu, largest first. Which municipality tops the table, and at roughly what total?
(d) In a comment: what does total_bu measure that Yield_bu_ac does not?


Answer

mb_rep <- mutate(mb_rep, total_bu = Acres * Yield_bu_ac)
mean(mb_rep$total_bu)
arrange(mb_rep, desc(total_bu))


Mean 382,865 bu.


PORTAGE LA PRAIRIE, at about 5.13 million bushels.


Production – how much grain the planting actually produced – rather than how well each acre yielded. A modest yield on enormous acres can out-produce a great yield on few.





Question 76
A bushel of wheat is 60 lb, so one bu/ac is about 0.0673 t/ha.
(a) Filter mb_rep to 2025, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Add a yield_t_ha column with mutate(), saving the result, and compute its mean.
(c) In a comment: the canola conversion factor in the chapters was 0.0560. Why is wheat’s different?


Answer

rep_2025 <- filter(mb_rep, Year == 2025)
nrow(rep_2025)
rep_2025 <- mutate(rep_2025, yield_t_ha = Yield_bu_ac * 0.0673)
mean(rep_2025$yield_t_ha)


438 rows.


Mean 4.58 t/ha.


A bushel is a volume standardized by weight per crop – wheat’s bushel is 60 lb and canola’s is 50 lb – so the bu/ac-to-t/ha factor differs crop by crop.





Question 77
(a) Sort mb_rep from highest yield to lowest, and report the municipality, variety, and year in the top row.
(b) Sort it from lowest to highest instead. What changes in the code?
(c) In a comment: after (a) and (b), is mb_rep itself now sorted? Why or why not?


Answer

arrange(mb_rep, desc(Yield_bu_ac))
arrange(mb_rep, Yield_bu_ac)


HILLSBURG-ROBLIN-SHELL RIVER, BOLLES <SEED DEPOT>, 2022, at 97.8 bu/ac.


Drop the desc().


No – neither sorted result was assigned; both were displayed and discarded.





Question 78
A script contains, in order:
filter(mb, Reported == FALSE)
suppressed <- filter(mb, Reported == FALSE)
(a) In a comment: what does each line do, and what appears in the console after each?
(b) Report nrow(suppressed) and nrow(mb).
(c) In a comment: the suppressed rows have no yields. What did MASC suppress them for, according to the dataset description?


Answer



Line 1 computes the suppressed rows and prints them, saving nothing. Line 2 computes the same thing and saves it as suppressed, printing nothing.


nrow(suppressed) is 2,960; nrow(mb) is still 5,358.


Too few farms grew that variety in that municipality – the value is withheld to protect individual farms’ privacy, not because it was never measured.





Question 79
(a) From mb_rep, filter to the municipality ALEXANDER, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Select Variety, Year, and Yield_bu_ac from it, saving again.
(c) Sort so the best observation is on top. Which variety was it, at what yield?


Answer

alexander <- filter(mb_rep, Municipality == "ALEXANDER")
nrow(alexander)
alexander <- select(alexander, Variety, Year, Yield_bu_ac)
arrange(alexander, desc(Yield_bu_ac))


17 rows.


AAC ELIE(BW931), at 90.9 bu/ac.





Question 80
(a) Using head(), display the first six rows of mb.
(b) Sort mb_rep by Acres in descending order into a new object, select its Municipality, Variety, Year, and Acres columns into another, and display the first six rows.
(c) In a comment: what does the top row of (b) tell you, and why did we sort mb_rep rather than mb?


Answer

head(mb)
by_acres <- arrange(mb_rep, desc(Acres))
big <- select(by_acres, Municipality, Variety, Year, Acres)
head(big)

(b, c) The biggest single planting is AAC BRANDON (BW 932) in PORTAGE LA PRAIRIE, 2020, at 74,604 acres. We sorted the reported rows because the suppressed rows have no acre values to sort on.

title: Module 2 — Test Bank
text:
Questions 81–90 · Canada Field Crops
These questions use the full statcan_field_crops.csv – thirteen crops by province, 2015–2025. Read it into an object called crops at the start of this block.

Question 81
(a) Filter crops to Saskatchewan, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) From it, select Year, Crop, and Yield_bu_ac, saving the result, and report its column names.
(c) In a comment: how many rows does crops itself still have, and why?


Answer

sask <- filter(crops, Province == "Saskatchewan")
nrow(sask)
sask_slim <- select(sask, Year, Crop, Yield_bu_ac)
names(sask_slim)


137 rows.


Year, Crop, Yield_bu_ac.


Still 1,067 – the functions return new data frames and leave the original untouched.





Question 82
(a) Filter to the three prairie provinces – Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba – using %in%, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Write the same filter with two |s and confirm the count matches.
(c) In a comment: which version is easier to read, and when does the difference grow?


Answer

prairie <- filter(crops, Province %in% c("Alberta", "Saskatchewan", "Manitoba"))
nrow(prairie)
prairie2 <- filter(crops, Province == "Alberta" | Province == "Saskatchewan" | Province == "Manitoba")
nrow(prairie2)

(a, b) 410 rows both ways.

%in% – one condition instead of a chain, and the gap widens with every extra value in the set.





Question 83
(a) Filter crops to Canola in 2025, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Sort it from highest yield to lowest. Which province tops the table, at what yield?
(c) In a comment: only seven provinces appear, not ten. What is the likely reason?


Answer

canola_25 <- filter(crops, Crop == "Canola" & Year == 2025)
nrow(canola_25)
arrange(canola_25, desc(Yield_bu_ac))


7 rows.


Ontario, at 49.8 bu/ac.


The other provinces grow too little canola for StatCan to publish an estimate – absent rows usually mean not grown or not reported, not zero.





Question 84
(a) Make a version of crops with only Year, Province, Crop, and Yield_bu_ac – once by naming what you keep, once by dropping Seeded_acres – saving each, and confirm the two match. Then keep the adjacent range Year:Crop and report its names.
(b) Rename Seeded_acres to acres, saving the result, and show the new column names.


Answer

kept    <- select(crops, Year, Province, Crop, Yield_bu_ac)
dropped <- select(crops, -Seeded_acres)
names(kept)
names(dropped)
ranged  <- select(crops, Year:Crop)
names(ranged)
renamed <- rename(crops, acres = Seeded_acres)
names(renamed)


Identical four names both ways; the range keeps Year, Province, Crop.


Year, Province, Crop, acres, Yield_bu_ac.





Question 85
(a) Filter crops to Spring wheat, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Add a seeded_m_acres column – seeded acres in millions (divide by 1,000,000) – with mutate(), saving the result.
(c) Compute the mean of the new column. In a comment: why might millions of acres be the better unit to report than raw acres?


Answer

spring <- filter(crops, Crop == "Spring wheat")
nrow(spring)
spring <- mutate(spring, seeded_m_acres = Seeded_acres / 1000000)
mean(spring$seeded_m_acres)


94 rows.


Mean 2.06 million acres – a reader can hold “about two million acres” in their head; a nine-digit raw number they cannot.





Question 86
(a) Filter to Saskatchewan spring wheat (all years), saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Add a total_bu column, seeded acres times yield, with mutate(), saving the result.
(c) Sort by total_bu, largest first. Which year tops the table, and at roughly what production?
(d) In a comment: could a year top this table without having the best yield? How?


Answer

sask_sw <- filter(crops, Province == "Saskatchewan" & Crop == "Spring wheat")
nrow(sask_sw)
sask_sw <- mutate(sask_sw, total_bu = Seeded_acres * Yield_bu_ac)
arrange(sask_sw, desc(total_bu))


11 rows.


2025, at about 490 million bushels.


Yes – production is acres times yield, so a big-acreage year with a middling yield can out-produce a small-acreage year with a great one.





Question 87
(a) Sort crops by Seeded_acres in descending order into a new object, select Province, Crop, Year, and Seeded_acres into another, and display the first six rows.
(b) In a comment: which province-crop combination fills the top of the table, and at what peak acreage?
(c) In a comment: the crop list contains both Wheat (all) and Spring wheat. What does that mean for anyone tempted to add acreages across crops?


Answer

by_acres <- arrange(crops, desc(Seeded_acres))
big <- select(by_acres, Province, Crop, Year, Seeded_acres)
head(big)


Saskatchewan’s Wheat (all), peaking at 14,178,100 acres in 2024.


The categories overlap – Wheat (all) already contains spring wheat, durum, and winter wheat – so summing acreage across crop rows would double-count. Check what each category includes before adding.





Question 88
A script contains, in order:
filter(crops, Province == "Manitoba")
manitoba <- filter(crops, Province == "Manitoba")
(a) In a comment: what does each line do, and what appears in the console after each?
(b) Report nrow(manitoba) and nrow(crops).
(c) In a comment: line 1’s printed result has scrolled out of the console. Is it stored anywhere you can get it back from?


Answer



Line 1 computes Manitoba’s rows and prints them, saving nothing; line 2 saves the same result as manitoba and prints nothing.


nrow(manitoba) is 137; nrow(crops) is still 1,067.


No – a displayed result that was never assigned is gone once it scrolls past. Only line 2’s manitoba can be brought back, which is the point of assigning.





Question 89
(a) Filter crops to Flax, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Select Province, Year, and Yield_bu_ac from it, saving again, and sort best-first. Which province and year top the list, at what yield?
(c) In a comment: only 39 flax rows exist across eleven years. What does that tell you about where flax is grown?


Answer

flax <- filter(crops, Crop == "Flax")
nrow(flax)
flax <- select(flax, Province, Year, Yield_bu_ac)
arrange(flax, desc(Yield_bu_ac))


39 rows.


Alberta in 2025, at 40.8 bu/ac.


Only three to six provinces (usually three) report it in any year – flax is a prairie specialty crop, not grown countrywide.





Question 90
(a) Using head(), display the first six rows of crops.
(b) Sort by Yield_bu_ac in descending order into a new object, select Crop, Province, Year, and Yield_bu_ac into another, and display the first six rows.
(c) In a comment: every top row is the same crop and province. Which, and why does a 180 bu/ac corn yield not mean corn “beats” wheat at 74?


Answer

head(crops)
by_yield <- arrange(crops, desc(Yield_bu_ac))
top <- select(by_yield, Crop, Province, Year, Yield_bu_ac)
head(top)

(b, c) All Ontario corn for grain, peaking at 180 bu/ac in 2024. Corn is simply a higher-bulk crop – and a corn bushel (56 lb) is not even the same quantity as a wheat bushel (60 lb), so cross-crop comparisons in bu/ac compare different things twice over.

title: Module 2 — Test Bank
text:
Questions 91–100 · Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields
Still the full eight-crop file (rm_yields).

Question 91
(a) Write a pipeline, one step per line with a short comment on each step, that filters rm_yields to Durum in 2025, keeps only the RM and Yield columns, and sorts the result from highest yield to lowest.
(b) Run it. How many rows are in the resulting data frame, and which RM had the best durum yield in 2025, at what value?
(c) In a comment: read your pipeline aloud as a “take the data, then …, then …, then …” sentence.


Answer

rm_yields |>                              # take the data, THEN
  filter(Crop == "Durum" & Year == 2025) |>  # keep durum in 2025, THEN
  select(RM, Yield) |>                    # keep two columns, THEN
  arrange(desc(Yield))                    # sort best-first


189 rows; RM 369 at 105.6 bu/ac.


Take rm_yields, then keep the 2025 durum rows, then keep the RM and Yield columns, then sort from highest yield to lowest.





Question 92
(a) In one pipeline, compute the mean flax yield across 2020–2025 (Year >= 2020), calling the result column mean_yield.
(b) Add n() to the same summarise() to count how many observations that mean is based on.
(c) In a comment: why is reporting the count alongside the mean good practice?


Answer

rm_yields |>
  filter(Crop == "Flax" & Year >= 2020) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield),
            n = n())

(a, b) Mean 22.39 bu/ac from 1,143 observations.

A mean based on a handful of rows deserves less trust than one based on a thousand; the count tells the reader which they are looking at.





Question 93
(a) In one pipeline, filter to Canola and summarise three things: the mean yield, the standard deviation, and the number of observations.
(b) Report the three values.
(c) In a comment: your result is a data frame. How many rows does it have, and what would mutate() have produced instead of summarise() here?


Answer

rm_yields |>
  filter(Crop == "Canola") |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield),
            sd_yield = sd(Yield),
            n = n())


Mean 28.29, sd 10.06, n 10,039.


One row. mutate() would have kept all 10,039 rows and repeated the overall mean on every one – summarise() collapses, mutate() adds.





Question 94
(a) In one pipeline, compute the mean yield and observation count for each crop, over the whole dataset.
(b) Which crop shows the largest mean, and roughly how far above the others is it?
(c) In a comment: why is that comparison meaningless as it stands, and which column proves it?


Answer

rm_yields |>
  group_by(Crop) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield),
            n = n())


Eight rows, one per crop: Barley 51.8, Canola 28.3, Durum 33.6, Flax 20.5, Lentils 1,208.4, Oats 64.7, Peas 31.8, Spring Wheat 35.3.


Lentils, at nearly twenty times the next-highest crop.


Lentils are measured in pounds per acre and everything else in bushels – the Unit column. The group means are each fine on their own terms; comparing them across the unit boundary is not.





Question 95
(a) In one pipeline, compute the mean canola yield for each year from 2021 to 2025 (filter first, then group).
(b) Report the five means. Which year was worst, and which best?
(c) In a comment: 2021 was a severe drought year in Saskatchewan. Does the data agree?


Answer

rm_yields |>
  filter(Crop == "Canola" & Year >= 2021) |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield))

(a, b) 2021 21.9, 2022 35.4, 2023 33.9, 2024 31.5, 2025 43.9. Worst 2021, best 2025.

Yes – the 2021 mean sits roughly a third below the surrounding years.





Question 96
(a) In one pipeline, compute each RM’s mean Spring Wheat yield across all years, and sort the result so the best wheat-growing RMs are on top.
(b) Report the top three RMs and their means.
(c) In a comment: your result has one row per RM. What did each row of the input represent, and what changed?


Answer

rm_yields |>
  filter(Crop == "Spring Wheat") |>
  group_by(RM) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_yield))


RM 369 (47.6), RM 333 (47.2), RM 368 (47.2).


Each input row was one RM-year-crop observation; group_by + summarise collapsed the years, leaving one row per RM.





Question 97
(a) In one pipeline: filter to Lentils, convert to kg/ha with mutate() (multiply by 1.12), then summarise the mean of the converted column.
(b) Report the mean in kg/ha.
(c) In a comment: in what order do your steps run, and why would putting the summarise() before the mutate() fail?


Answer

rm_yields |>
  filter(Crop == "Lentils") |>
  mutate(yield_kg_ha = Yield * 1.12) |>
  summarise(mean_kg_ha = mean(yield_kg_ha))


1,353.4 kg/ha.


Top to bottom – each step’s output feeds the next. After summarise() the data has collapsed to one row and the yield_kg_ha column would not exist yet to summarise.





Question 98
A classmate hands you this pipeline and asks what it does:
rm_yields |>
  filter(Crop %in% c("Oats", "Barley") & Year >= 2015) |>
  group_by(Crop) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield),
            n = n())
(a) In a comment: explain the pipeline step by step, one sentence per step.
(b) Run it and report the output.
(c) In a comment: answer the classmate’s real question in plain language – what does the output say about oats and barley since 2015?


Answer



Take the data; keep only oat and barley rows from 2015 on; split those rows into the two crops; collapse each crop to its mean yield and its number of observations.


Barley 60.5 bu/ac (n = 3,131); Oats 79.5 bu/ac (n = 2,434).


Since 2015, oat yields have averaged about 19 bu/ac higher than barley yields across Saskatchewan RMs, based on several thousand observations of each.





Question 99
This pipeline was meant to find low- and high-yielding canola observations – below 15 or above 55 bu/ac – but it returns zero rows:
rm_yields |>
  filter(Crop == "Canola") |>
  filter(Yield < 15 & Yield > 55) |>
  arrange(desc(Yield))
(a) In a comment: apply the module’s debugging habit – which step do you run first, and what do you check at each step?
(b) In a comment: identify the broken step and explain why it returns nothing.
(c) Write the corrected pipeline.
(d) In a comment: your corrected pipeline works, but a classmate’s copy of it still gives odd results even though their code now matches yours. What does the module say to try before hunting further?


Answer



Run the first step alone and check the result looks right (the canola rows), then add the second step and check again – the first step where the data stops looking right is the problem.


The second filter: & demands both conditions true of the same row, and no yield is simultaneously below 15 and above 55. The question said “or”.


Replace & with |: filter(Yield < 15 | Yield > 55).


Restart R and run the script from the top in a fresh session – leftover objects from the console, or stale versions of a data frame, disappear on a clean run.





Question 100
(a) In one pipeline: for 2025 only, compute each crop’s mean yield and observation count, sorted from highest mean to lowest, and save the result as crop_summary_2025.
(b) Write the table to output/crop_summary_2025.csv.
(c) Report the two highest-yielding crops in the sorted table. In a comment: why does the crop in first place not mean what it appears to mean, and which crop is really the standout?


Answer

crop_summary_2025 <- rm_yields |>
  filter(Year == 2025) |>
  group_by(Crop) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield),
            n = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_yield))

write_csv(crop_summary_2025, "output/crop_summary_2025.csv")

(a, c) Lentils top the table at 1,897 – but that is pounds per acre, not bushels. Among the bushel crops, Oats lead at 97.5 bu/ac (Barley next at 72.8). 2025 was a strong year across the board.

title: Module 2 — Test Bank
text:
Questions 101–110 · Manitoba Wheat Variety
Full mb_wheat_varieties.csv, read as mb, with the reported rows saved as mb_rep <- filter(mb, Reported == TRUE) at the start of this block. Build everything else as pipelines.

Question 101
(a) Write a pipeline, one step per line with a short comment on each, that filters mb_rep to 2025, keeps Municipality, Variety, and Yield_bu_ac, and sorts best-first.
(b) Run it. How many rows are in the resulting data frame, and which municipality and variety top it, at what yield?
(c) In a comment: read the pipeline aloud as a “take the data, then …” sentence.


Answer

mb_rep |>                                          # take the reported rows, THEN
  filter(Year == 2025) |>                          # keep 2025, THEN
  select(Municipality, Variety, Yield_bu_ac) |>    # keep three columns, THEN
  arrange(desc(Yield_bu_ac))                       # sort best-first


438 rows; LOUISE, growing SY MANNESS, at 96.3 bu/ac.


Take the reported rows, then keep 2025, then keep three columns, then sort from highest yield to lowest.





Question 102
(a) In one pipeline, compute the mean of Yield_bu_ac across all of mb_rep, calling it mean_yield, together with n().
(b) Report both values.
(c) In a comment: why report the count alongside the mean?


Answer

mb_rep |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield_bu_ac),
            n = n())


Mean 61.16 bu/ac from 2,398 observations.


A mean earns trust in proportion to what it is based on; the count tells the reader how much that is.





Question 103
(a) In one pipeline, filter mb_rep to the variety AAC STARBUCK <SECAN> and summarise its mean yield, standard deviation, and observation count.
(b) Report the three values.
(c) In a comment: how many rows does your result have, and what would mutate() have produced in place of summarise()?


Answer

mb_rep |>
  filter(Variety == "AAC STARBUCK <SECAN>") |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield_bu_ac),
            sd_yield = sd(Yield_bu_ac),
            n = n())


Mean 62.7, sd 11.28, n 374.


One row. mutate() would have kept all 374 rows with the summary repeated on each – summarise() collapses, mutate() adds.





Question 104
(a) In one pipeline, compute each variety’s mean yield and observation count across mb_rep, sorted from highest mean to lowest.
(b) Report the top two varieties, their means, and their counts.
(c) In a comment: the second-place variety was observed exactly once. Which first-place claim would you trust more, and why?


Answer

mb_rep |>
  group_by(Variety) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield_bu_ac),
            n = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_yield))


AAC WESTKING, 79.2 bu/ac from 17 observations; then CDC GO (BW781), 77.5 from 1.


WESTKING’s – seventeen municipality-years is evidence; a single observation could be one lucky field in one good year.





Question 105
(a) In one pipeline, compute the mean reported yield for each year, 2020 through 2025.
(b) Report the six means. Which year was worst, and which best?
(c) In a comment: the RM dataset showed Saskatchewan canola cratering in 2021. Does Manitoba wheat agree about that year?


Answer

mb_rep |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield_bu_ac))

(a, b) 2020 62.4, 2021 49.6, 2022 59.8, 2023 61.4, 2024 64.7, 2025 68.0. Worst 2021, best 2025.

Yes – 2021 sits ten to fifteen bushels below every other year. The drought was prairie-wide, not a Saskatchewan quirk.





Question 106
(a) In one pipeline, compute each municipality’s mean reported yield, sorted best-first.
(b) Report the top three municipalities and their means.
(c) In a comment: what did each row of the input represent, and what does each row of the result represent?


Answer

mb_rep |>
  group_by(Municipality) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield_bu_ac)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_yield))


LOUISE (72.9), LAC DU BONNET (71.5), ALEXANDER (71.4).


Each input row was one variety in one municipality in one year; each result row is one municipality, its varieties and years collapsed into a single mean.





Question 107
A bushel of wheat is 60 lb, so one bu/ac is about 0.0673 t/ha.
(a) In one pipeline: convert mb_rep’s yields to t/ha with mutate(), then compute the mean t/ha for each year.
(b) Report the 2021 and 2025 values.
(c) In a comment: why must the mutate() step come before the summarise() step?


Answer

mb_rep |>
  mutate(yield_t_ha = Yield_bu_ac * 0.0673) |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(mean_t_ha = mean(yield_t_ha))


2021 3.34 t/ha; 2025 4.58 t/ha.


Each step’s output feeds the next – after summarise() the data has collapsed to one row per year and the yield_t_ha column would not exist to average.





Question 108
A classmate hands you this pipeline and asks what it does:
mb_rep |>
  filter(Yield_bu_ac > 70) |>
  group_by(Variety) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
(a) In a comment: explain it step by step, one sentence per step.
(b) Run it and report the top three rows.
(c) In a comment: answer the real question in plain language – what does the output say?


Answer



Take the reported rows; keep only observations over 70 bu/ac; split them by variety; count each variety’s rows; sort the counts largest-first.


AAC STARBUCK <SECAN> 102, AAC WHEATLAND <SECAN> 82, AAC BRANDON (BW 932) 73.


When Manitoba wheat topped 70 bu/ac, it was most often Starbuck doing it – these three varieties account for most of the high-yield observations.





Question 109
This pipeline was meant to find AAC Brandon’s reported observations, but it returns zero rows:
mb_rep |>
  filter(Variety == "aac brandon (bw 932)") |>
  arrange(desc(Yield_bu_ac))
(a) In a comment: apply the debugging habit – what do you run first, and what do you check?
(b) In a comment: identify the problem and say why R found nothing, with no error.
(c) Write the corrected pipeline.


Answer



Run the filter step alone and look at its result – it returns zero rows, so the problem is there, not in the sort.


Text matching is exact, capitals included. The data stores the variety in capitals, so the lowercase string matches no row – and a filter that matches nothing is not an error, just an empty result.


mb_rep |> filter(Variety == "AAC BRANDON (BW 932)") |> arrange(desc(Yield_bu_ac)).





Question 110
(a) In one pipeline: for 2025 only, compute each variety’s mean reported yield and observation count, sorted best-first, and save the result as variety_summary_2025.
(b) Write the table to output/variety_summary_2025.csv.
(c) Report the top row. In a comment: the table also contains varieties observed only twice – what should a reader keep in mind when comparing rows?


Answer

variety_summary_2025 <- mb_rep |>
  filter(Year == 2025) |>
  group_by(Variety) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield_bu_ac),
            n = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_yield))

write_csv(variety_summary_2025, "output/variety_summary_2025.csv")


AAC WESTKING, 79.2 bu/ac from 17 observations. Rows with tiny counts (some varieties appear once or twice) carry far less evidence than their neighbours – the n column is part of the answer, not decoration.

title: Module 2 — Test Bank
text:
Questions 111–120 · Canada Field Crops
Full statcan_field_crops.csv, read as crops at the start of this block. Build everything as pipelines.

Question 111
(a) Write a pipeline, one step per line with a short comment on each, that filters crops to Canola, keeps Province, Year, and Yield_bu_ac, and sorts best-first.
(b) Run it. How many rows, and which province-year tops the table, at what yield?
(c) In a comment: before declaring that province Canada’s canola capital, what other column in the dataset would you look at, and why?


Answer

crops |>                                    # take the data, THEN
  filter(Crop == "Canola") |>               # keep canola, THEN
  select(Province, Year, Yield_bu_ac) |>    # keep three columns, THEN
  arrange(desc(Yield_bu_ac))                # sort best-first


75 rows; New Brunswick in 2024, at 54.2 bu/ac. (One row, Prince Edward Island 2021, has a missing yield; arrange() puts missing values last, so the sort is unaffected.)


Seeded_acres – a tiny acreage can post a great average that means little next to Saskatchewan’s millions of acres. Best yield and biggest grower are different titles.





Question 112
(a) In one pipeline, filter to Spring wheat and summarise the mean yield, the standard deviation, and the observation count.
(b) Report the three values.
(c) In a comment: say what the standard deviation means here, for a reader who farms.


Answer

crops |>
  filter(Crop == "Spring wheat") |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield_bu_ac),
            sd_yield = sd(Yield_bu_ac),
            n = n())


Mean 51.32 bu/ac, sd 7.52, from 94 province-years.


A typical province-year sits within about seven or eight bushels of the 51 bu/ac average – the spread across provinces and years, not field-to-field variation.





Question 113
(a) In one pipeline, filter to Saskatchewan spring wheat and summarise the mean yield and count.
(b) Report both values.
(c) In a comment: Saskatchewan’s mean sits about five bushels below the all-province average of 51.3 bu/ac. How can the country’s biggest wheat grower not have its best yields?


Answer

crops |>
  filter(Province == "Saskatchewan" & Crop == "Spring wheat") |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield_bu_ac),
            n = n())


Mean 46.6 bu/ac from 11 years.


Acreage and yield measure different things – Saskatchewan farms vast dryland acres, including land drier than anything a smaller, wetter province would put into wheat. Growing the most and yielding the most per acre are separate claims.





Question 114
(a) In one pipeline, compute each province’s mean spring wheat yield, with counts, sorted best-first.
(b) Report the top three provinces.
(c) In a comment: what does each row of the result represent, and how many years does each mean average over?


Answer

crops |>
  filter(Crop == "Spring wheat") |>
  group_by(Province) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield_bu_ac),
            n = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_yield))


Manitoba (59.0), Ontario (56.6), Alberta (52.3).


One row per province, its years collapsed into a single mean. Most provinces contribute all eleven years (n = 11), but not all – Nova Scotia has spring wheat estimates for only six, which is what the n column is there to show.





Question 115
(a) In one pipeline, compute the national mean spring wheat yield for each year, 2015 through 2025.
(b) Which year was worst, and which best, at what values?
(c) In a comment: both other datasets in this bank flagged the same worst year. What is the year, and what does agreement across three independent datasets tell you?


Answer

crops |>
  filter(Crop == "Spring wheat") |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield_bu_ac))


Worst 2021 at 45.7; best 2022 at 56.5.


2021 – the prairie drought. When three datasets collected by different agencies point at the same year, the signal is in the world, not in any one file.





Question 116
(a) In one pipeline, compute each province’s mean spring wheat seeded acres, sorted largest-first.
(b) Report the top three.
(c) In a comment: on mean yield, Manitoba leads the provinces at 59.0 bu/ac and Saskatchewan trails the prairies. Compare that ordering with this table – what changes, and what does that say about “best wheat province” as a phrase?


Answer

crops |>
  filter(Crop == "Spring wheat") |>
  group_by(Province) |>
  summarise(mean_acres = mean(Seeded_acres)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_acres))


Saskatchewan (8.03M acres), Alberta (6.23M), Manitoba (2.99M).


The order flips – Manitoba leads on yield but is third on acres, Saskatchewan the reverse. “Best” depends entirely on whether you mean per-acre performance or total scale.





Question 117
(a) In one pipeline: filter to Spring wheat, create total_bu (seeded acres times yield) with mutate(), then compute each province’s mean total_bu, sorted largest-first.
(b) Report the top province and its rough value.
(c) In a comment: why must the mutate() come before the group_by()/summarise() pair?


Answer

crops |>
  filter(Crop == "Spring wheat") |>
  mutate(total_bu = Seeded_acres * Yield_bu_ac) |>
  group_by(Province) |>
  summarise(mean_total_bu = mean(total_bu)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_total_bu))


Saskatchewan, at about 377 million bushels a year.


summarise() collapses the rows – the per-row total_bu has to exist before the collapse, or there is nothing to average.





Question 118
A classmate hands you this pipeline:
crops |>
  filter(Province %in% c("Alberta", "Saskatchewan", "Manitoba") &
           Crop == "Spring wheat" & Year >= 2020) |>
  group_by(Province) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield_bu_ac),
            n = n())
(a) In a comment: explain it step by step.
(b) Run it and report the output.
(c) In a comment: answer in plain language – what does it say about prairie wheat since 2020?


Answer



Take the data; keep prairie-province spring wheat rows from 2020 on; split them by province; report each province’s mean yield and row count.


Alberta 51.2 (n = 6), Manitoba 60.9 (n = 6), Saskatchewan 47.3 (n = 6).


Since 2020, Manitoba’s spring wheat has out-yielded Alberta’s by about ten bushels an acre and Saskatchewan’s by about thirteen – each figure an average over six years.





Question 119
This pipeline was meant to compute each province’s average spring wheat production, but it stops with object 'Seeded_acres' not found:
crops |>
  filter(Crop == "Spring wheat") |>
  group_by(Province) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield_bu_ac)) |>
  mutate(total_bu = Seeded_acres * Yield_bu_ac)
(a) In a comment: apply the debugging habit – run the pipeline one step at a time. After which step does Seeded_acres stop existing, and how can you tell?
(b) In a comment: identify the bug and state the general rule it breaks.
(c) Write the corrected pipeline (its last step should report each province’s mean total_bu).


Answer



After the summarise() step – run the pipeline up to each |> and look at the columns. Once summarise() runs, the data has collapsed to Province and mean_yield; Seeded_acres and Yield_bu_ac are gone, so the mutate() has nothing to work with.


mutate() builds per-row columns, so it must come before the collapse – the order of pipeline steps matters because each step works on the previous step’s output.





crops |>
  filter(Crop == "Spring wheat") |>
  mutate(total_bu = Seeded_acres * Yield_bu_ac) |>
  group_by(Province) |>
  summarise(mean_total_bu = mean(total_bu))



Question 120
(a) In one pipeline: for Spring wheat across all years, compute each province’s mean yield and count, sorted best-first, and save the result as wheat_by_province.
(b) Write the table to output/wheat_by_province.csv.
(c) Report the top row. In a comment: a reader sees Manitoba first and concludes “Manitoba grows Canada’s wheat.” Saskatchewan seeds about 8 million acres of spring wheat a year to Manitoba’s 3 million – say precisely what is wrong with that sentence.


Answer

wheat_by_province <- crops |>
  filter(Crop == "Spring wheat") |>
  group_by(Province) |>
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(Yield_bu_ac),
            n = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_yield))

write_csv(wheat_by_province, "output/wheat_by_province.csv")


Manitoba, 59.0 bu/ac (n = 11). Manitoba grows wheat best per acre; Saskatchewan grows Canada’s wheat, seeding nearly three times Manitoba’s acres. Yield tables and scale tables answer different questions, and this table is only the first kind.
